uses: Immature raw green jackfruit cooked as a hearty fibrous vegetable ('tree meat' / kathal ki sabzi)
Sweet ripe bulbs consumed fresh, fried into chips, or preserved in sugar syrups
Hard, termite-resistant yellow heartwood prized for musical instruments (veena, mridangam) and temple furniture
careTips: Requires spacious acreage in warm, frost-free humid tropical conditions
Needs deep, rich, porous alluvial soils with unobstructed drainage
Protect young saplings from livestock grazing and waterlogging
46.toxicityNote: Fruit bulbs and seeds are edible and nutritious once cooked. Sticky white latex contains mechanical irritants that can cause mild localized skin itching in sensitive individuals; raw unripened fruit should be boiled before consumption
46.funFact: Jackfruit is the largest tree-borne fruit on the planet, with exceptional specimens reaching over 55 kilograms in weight and nearly a meter in length.

47.description: A long-lived, massive shade tree with a broad rounded canopy of feathery pinnate foliage, weeping branches, and pendulous curved brown pods containing tart, sticky pulp.
identifyingFeatures: Graceful, dense spreading canopy with finely pinnate compound leaves (10-20 pairs of small leaflets)
Small yellow flowers with red or orange veins borne in lax racemes
Curved, cinnamon-brown brittle sausage-shaped pods filled with tart, fibrous brown sticky pulp and glossy hard brown seeds
47.habitat: Dry tropical savannahs, roadsides, agricultural village borders, and pasture clearings.
47.distribution: Native to tropical Africa; introduced to India millennia ago where it naturalized so deeply that Linnaeus named it 'indica'.
uses: Quintessential souring agent in Indian cuisine for sambar, rasam, imli chutney, and street pani puri
Tartaric acid pulp traditionally rubbed to polish and restore the shine of brass and copper sacred idols
Deep, cooling roadside avenue shade tree across national highways
careTips: Requires full direct sun and thrives in deep alluvial or gravelly soils
Remarkably drought and wind resistant once mature due to immense taproots
Prune young trees to establish a high central trunk clear of low traffic
47.toxicityNote: Completely non-toxic; pulp, tender young leaves, and roasted seeds are edible and safe for humans and animals.
47.funFact: The name Tamarind derives from the Arabic 'Tamar-ul-Hind', literally translating to 'Date of India', referencing the dark, sticky, date-like pulp inside the pods.

48.description: A majestic, fast-growing evergreen tree revered in Indian mythology and Ayurveda, bearing glossy aromatic leaves, fragrant white blossoms, and deep purple-black sweet-astringent berries.
identifyingFeatures: Rough, cracked grey bark and dense rounded evergreen canopy with pink-tinged young flushes
Opposite, oblong-ovate leathery leaves with a faint turpentine scent when crushed
Clusters of small fragrant greenish-white flowers with prominent stamens
Ovoid berry-like drupes turning from green to magenta and finally deep glossy purplish-black with dark staining flesh
48.habitat: Riverbanks, moist deciduous forests, marsh edges, and rural avenue roadsides.
48.distribution: Native to the Indian subcontinent and Southeast Asia; sacred tree of Jambudvipa ('continent of the Jamun tree').
uses: Delicious summer fruit eaten fresh with black salt (kala namak) or made into vinegar and juices

Dried seed powder (Jamun gutli) is documented in ethnopharmacological and clinical studies; active gallic acid and jamboline inhibit alpha-amylase and alpha-glucosidase, providing supportive complementary glycemic regulation in type 2 diabetes under medical guidance
Durable, water-resistant timber used for railway sleepers, well-linings, and agricultural tools
careTips: Thrives in rich, moist alluvial soils near canals or river systems, but also tolerates seasonal drought
Needs full overhead sun for prolific summer fruiting
Protect ripening fruit from parakeet and bat flocks
48.toxicityNote: Non-toxic; fruit and seeds are safe in dietary use. The anthocyanins in fruit heavily stain tongues and clothing dark purple.
48.funFact: In ancient Hindu cosmology, the Indian subcontinent was known as 'Jambudvipa' (the Island of the Jambu Trees), named after the abundance of giant Jamun trees.

49.description: A handsome, slow-growing evergreen tree with dense glossy foliage, famed for its scurfy brown egg-shaped fruit with sweet, brown sugar-flavored malty grainy pulp.
identifyingFeatures: Dense, pyramidal-to-rounded canopy of glossy, dark green elliptic leathery leaves clustered at branch tips
Copious white gummy milky latex (chicle) throughout bark, stems, and unripe fruit
Round to oval scurfy brownish-sandpaper fruits containing soft, caramel-sweet brown flesh and 2-5 hard shiny black seeds
49.habitat: Coastal tropical plains, warm orchards, and coastal sandy loam plantations.
49.distribution: Native to southern Mexico and Central America; naturalized and massively grown in western India (Gujarat, Maharashtra, Karnataka).
uses: Delectable dessert fruit eaten chilled, blended into thick chikoo milkshakes, or dried into fruit slices
Historical commercial source of 'chicle', the natural latex gum base used to make chewing gum
Wind-resistant coastal agroforestry shelterbelt tree
careTips: Requires warm, tropical coastal climate and full sun for sweet fruit development
Highly adaptable to diverse soils including saline coastal soils and limestone loams
Water regularly during fruit set; drought-tolerant once established
49.toxicityNote: Ripe fruit pulp is delicious and non-toxic. The hard black seeds have a sharp protruding apical hook that can snag in the esophageal or pharyngeal lining if swallowed whole, posing a mechanical foreign body risk
49.funFact: The milky latex tapped from wild Sapodilla trunks was the original raw ingredient for Adams Chiclets, pioneering the modern global chewing gum industry.

50.description: A small, semi-deciduous tropical fruit tree bearing irregular rounded fruits with a knobby, bumpy scale-like exterior and luscious creamy, fragrant custard-like white segments.
identifyingFeatures: Irregular small branching tree with dull green, lanceolate alternate leaves emitting an odd musky scent when crushed
Thick, fleshy, three-sided nodding greenish-yellow flowers hanging from leaf axils
Globose greenish syncarp covered in rounded, protruding knobby fleshy scales that separate when ripe
Soft, fragrant, sweet creamy-white pulp surrounding numerous smooth, shiny dark-brown to black seeds
50.habitat: Dry scrublands, rocky hillsides, homestead gardens, and arid marginal soils.
50.distribution: Native to tropical Americas and West Indies; widely cultivated across central and southern India.
uses: Prized seasonal dessert fruit eaten fresh, blended into Sitaphal ice creams, or pureed into rabdi

Crushed seeds and leaf extracts contain bioactive acetogenins (annonacin) and aporphine alkaloids with confirmed pediculicidal (anti-lice) and insecticidal properties; must be kept strictly away from eyes to prevent corneal ulceration
High natural source of Vitamin C, dietary fiber, magnesium, and potassium
careTips: Thrives in hot, dry climates with excellent soil drainage; cannot tolerate frost or waterlogged roots
Performs surprisingly well on rocky, gravelly, and low-fertility hillsides
Harvest fruits when the skin fissures between scales turn pale creamy-white
50.toxicityNote: PULP IS EDIBLE. SEEDS AND LEAVES ARE TOXIC: Seeds contain neurotoxic annonacin and acetogenins; crushed seeds cause severe eye inflammation and are toxic if swallowed or chewed. Keep seeds away from children and pets.
50.funFact: Custard apple is commonly known as 'Sitaphal' in India, traditionally associated with Sita from the epic Ramayana.

51.description: A thorny evergreen citrus tree producing fragrant white-and-purple blossoms, glossy leaves with winged petioles, and oval yellow-green fruits filled with sour, acidic juice.
identifyingFeatures: Spreading thorny branches armed with stout, sharp stiff spines in leaf axils
Elliptic dark green leathery leaves with translucent oil glands that release a sharp citrus fragrance
Sweetly fragrant white blossoms with purple-flushed petals and yellow stamens
Ovoid yellow-to-green hesperidium fruits with a mamillate nipple at apex and acidic juice vesicles
51.habitat: Sunny orchards, suburban backyards, terrace pots, and warm agricultural valleys.
51.distribution: Native to Northeast India, Northern Myanmar, and China; cultivated ubiquitously across India and the globe.
uses: Indispensable culinary citrus for salads, nimbu pani (lemonade), dal seasonings, and traditional spicy pickles
Rich source of dietary Vitamin C and citric acid used for digestive drinks and home cleansing
Essential component of Indian good-luck charms (nimbu-mirchi toran) hung on doors and vehicles
careTips: Requires at least 6-8 hours of direct unfiltered sunlight daily
Provide light, well-draining sandy loam; avoid wet feet to prevent phytophthora gummosis
Feed quarterly with citrus-specific micronutrient fertilizers containing zinc, iron, and magnesium
51.toxicityNote: Fruit juice and zest are safe food ingredients. Cold-pressed peel essential oils contain furanocoumarins (psoralens) that cause severe phototoxic dermatitis (phytophotodermatitis) when skin exposed to the oil meets sunlight; limonene is toxic to cats and dogs if ingested in volume.
51.funFact: Genetic studies reveal that the cultivated lemon is actually an ancient hybrid between the sour orange (Citrus × aurantium) and the citron (Citrus medica).

sources.name: ASPCA Animal Poison Control & European Commission SCCS

52.description: A magnificent deciduous tropical hardwood tree famed worldwide for its gigantic rough leaves, huge panicles of tiny white flowers, and unparalleled termite-proof golden-brown timber.
identifyingFeatures: Tall, straight columnar trunk with fibrous, vertically grooved grey-brown bark
Massive, opposite, rough sandpaper-textured broadly elliptic leaves up to 40-70 cm long
Immense erect branched terminal panicles held above the canopy bearing thousands of tiny white flowers
Inflated, bladder-like papery calyx enclosing a hard globose four-celled woody nut
52.habitat: Moist and dry deciduous tropical forests, hilly slopes, and managed timber plantations.
52.distribution: Native to India, Myanmar, Laos, and Thailand; iconic heritage timber tree of peninsular India.
uses: World standard luxury timber for shipbuilding, exterior decking, high-end doors, and heirloom furniture
Exceptional natural resistance to rotting, weathering, termites, and marine borers due to high tectoquinone content
Folk use of leaf extracts as topical compresses for minor cutaneous sores is supported by in vitro antibacterial assays against Staphylococcus aureus, driven by quinone metabolites
careTips: Requires vast open forestry plots with deep, well-drained alluvial or basaltic soils
Needs blazing tropical sunshine and distinct dry and wet monsoon seasons
Long-term forestry investment requiring 20 to 30 years to reach harvestable heartwood girth
52.toxicityNote: Non-toxic in ordinary contact. Fine wood sawdust generated during carpentry contains lapachol and tectoquinone, potent sensitizers that trigger occupational contact dermatitis, conjunctivitis, and allergic respiratory rhinitis in exposed workers
52.funFact: Teak wood contains natural rubber oils and tectoquinone, making it so naturally waterproof and insect-resistant that teak ships built over 200 years ago still float soundly today.

53.description: A towering, slow-growing hardwood tree dominating the moist deciduous forests of northern and central India, famous for its dense timber, resinous dammar, and winged spiraling seeds.
identifyingFeatures: Tall straight cylindrical bole with thick, dark brown bark deeply furrowed with longitudinal fissures
Large, leathery, ovate-oblong alternate leaves with a rounded base and prominent parallel lateral veins
Creamy-white to pale yellowish fragrant flowers borne in large terminal and axillary racemose panicles
Nut-like fruit surrounded by 5 unequal elongated papery wings that helicopter down during seed dispersal
53.habitat: Terai foothills, sub-Himalayan forest belts, central Indian plateau reserves (Chota Nagpur).
53.distribution: Native to the Indian subcontinent (foothills of the Himalayas, eastern and central India).
uses: Heavy-duty timber used extensively for railway ties, structural beams, bridge construction, and mine props
Leaves stitched into ubiquitous durable traditional dining plates and bowls (patravali / donas)
Resin (Raal / Sal dammar) burned as sacred temple incense and used in traditional waterproofing
careTips: Suited only for large-scale natural forest conservation and forestry silviculture
Requires deep, well-aerated sandy loam soils; sensitive to prolonged stagnant waterlogging
Seeds have extremely short viability (days) and must germinate immediately upon falling at monsoon onset
53.toxicityNote: Non-toxic; leaves and resin are safe and traditionally utilized in incense and food serving.
53.funFact: According to Buddhist tradition, Queen Maya gave birth to Gautama Buddha under a blooming Sal tree in Lumbini garden, and Buddha passed into Parinirvana beneath a pair of Sal trees in Kushinagar.

54.description: A large, vigorous clump-forming giant woody grass with towering hollow culms, gracefully arching feathery foliage, and phenomenal, rapid daily growth rates.
identifyingFeatures: Dense, non-invasive sympodial (clumping) habit with stout, erect hollow culms up to 10-20 m high
Bright green to golden-yellow culms often striped with dark green vertical bands, ringed with node rings
Linear-lanceolate leaf blades with rough margins borne on short petioles along clustered branches
54.habitat: Tropical riverbanks, moist valleys, village groves, and managed agroforestry plantations.
54.distribution: Native to tropical Asia (Indo-Malayan region); widely naturalized and cultivated pantropically.
uses: Universal green building material ('green gold') for scaffolding, rural housing, fencing, and furniture
Tender emerging young shoots fermented, boiled, and cooked into savory traditional curries and pickles
Major industrial raw material for paper pulp manufacturing and eco-friendly textiles
careTips: Requires spacious garden areas or farm boundaries in full sun with plentiful soil moisture
Prefers rich, humusy loam with good drainage; avoid soggy saline soils
Thin out older culms (over 3-4 years old) to encourage robust new culm emergence during monsoon
54.toxicityNote: Raw emerging bamboo shoots contain cyanogenic glycosides (taxiphyllin) and MUST be thoroughly boiled or fermented to dissipate hydrogen cyanide before eating. Cooked shoots and mature culms are safe.
54.funFact: Certain bamboo species can grow up to 90 centimeters (almost 3 feet) in a single 24-hour period during peak monsoon season, making them the fastest-growing woody plants on Earth.

55.description: An elegant, tall, solitary feather palm with a slender ringed trunk, a compact crownshaft of dark green pinnate fronds, and hanging clusters of fibrous orange betel nuts.
identifyingFeatures: Extremely slender, perfectly straight columnar trunk reaching 15-25 m tall, marked with prominent pale circular rings
Neat, smooth olive-green crownshaft bearing a compact crown of arching pinnate fronds with crowded leaflets
Heavily branched spadix inflorescence emerging below the crownshaft, bearing dozens of oval green-to-orange fibrous nuts
55.habitat: Humid coastal belts, tropical valleys, homestead orchards, and high-rainfall Western Ghats plantations.
55.distribution: Native to tropical Asia and the Pacific; cultivated extensively across Kerala, Karnataka, Assam, and West Bengal.
uses: Cured nut (Supari) chewed with betel leaf (Paan), slaked lime, and spices as an age-old social stimulant
Indispensable sacred offering in Hindu Vedic rituals, pujas, and wedding blessings
Fallen sheaths molded into eco-friendly biodegradable dining plates and takeout bowls
careTips: Requires high atmospheric humidity, warm tropical temperatures, and abundant year-round water
Prefers deep, fertile clay loam or lateritic soils with good drainage; cannot endure waterlogging
Intercropped traditionally with black pepper vines, cardamom, and banana plants for optimal microclimate
55.toxicityNote: CARCINOGENIC WHEN CHEWED: Areca nut contains the alkaloid arecoline. The International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC) classifies areca nut as a Group 1 human carcinogen, strongly linked to oral submucous fibrosis and oral cancer. Chewing is hazardous to health.
55.funFact: Betel nut chewing is one of the world's oldest psychoactive traditions, practiced by hundreds of millions of people across South Asia and the Pacific for thousands of years.

56.description: An ancient, rugged desert feather palm with a stout diamond-patterned trunk, stiff grey-green spiny fronds, and heavy pendulous clusters of sweet, energy-rich dates.
identifyingFeatures: Stout columnar trunk up to 20-30 meters tall, covered in the persistent diamond-shaped bases of fallen fronds
Crown of stiff, arching, greyish-blue-green pinnate fronds with sharp, formidable spines at petiole base
Dioecious flowering (male and female trees separate); female palms produce heavy pendulous orange-to-brown fruit clusters
56.habitat: Arid desert oases, dry riverbeds, semi-arid agricultural lands, and desert margins.
56.distribution: Native to the Fertile Crescent and North Africa; cultivated across arid western India (Rajasthan, Gujarat, Kutch).
uses: Sweet, highly nutritious dried and fresh dates rich in sugars, fiber, iron, and potassium
Sap tapped in winter from related palms (Phoenix sylvestris) boiled into prized Bengal Khejur Gur (date palm jaggery)
Fronds used for making mats, baskets, fans, and traditional thatched roofing
careTips: Requires hot, dry desert conditions ('feet in water, head in the fire of heaven') with intense sun
Highly drought and salinity tolerant once established
Hand pollination of female inflorescences is commonly practiced in commercial cultivation to ensure high fruit set
56.toxicityNote: Non-toxic; fruit is completely wholesome. Caution: base of fronds armed with needle-sharp, rigid spines capable of puncturing skin.
56.funFact: Archaeological evidence shows date palm cultivation dating back more than 6,000 years in Mesopotamia, making it one of the oldest cultivated fruit trees in human civilization.

57.description: A gigantic, dramatic deciduous rainforest tree with massive plank buttress roots, spiny trunk, and blazing scarlet cup-shaped flowers that bloom on bare branches in late winter.
identifyingFeatures: Massive straight trunk with formidable conical prickles on younger bark and colossal buttress root fins at base
Palmately compound leaves with 5-7 lanceolate leaflets radiating like fingers from a central point
Spectacular, large fleshy scarlet-red flowers (10-15 cm wide) with recurved petals and a dense cluster of purple-black stamens
Large woody ellipsoid capsules that burst open when ripe, releasing clouds of fluffy white silky kapok fiber
57.habitat: Tropical wet and dry deciduous forests, alluvial flood plains, and rural roadsides.
57.distribution: Native to tropical South Asia and Southeast Asia; widely distributed across the Indian plains.
uses: Silky kapok fiber from seed pods harvested to stuff luxury pillows, cushions, and life vests (naturally buoyant and water-repellent)
Fleshy flower calyces cooked as a prized seasonal vegetable (Semal ke doke) in northern India
Classical Ayurvedic gum exudate (Mocharas) and young taproots (Semal musli) contain dense mucilage and tannins utilized traditionally as cooling astringents and demulcents for diarrhea and hemoptysis
careTips: Requires vast acreage due to enormous canopy and massive surface buttress roots
Plant in full direct sun with deep, moist alluvial or riverbank soil
Deciduous in winter; drops leaves completely before producing flaming floral canopy in February-March
57.toxicityNote: Non-toxic; flowers, young pods, and gum have traditional culinary and medicinal uses. Safe around pets.
57.funFact: When in bloom on bare branches, a single Semal tree becomes a bustling wildlife hub, attracting dozens of bird species, fruit bats, and monkeys gorging on abundant nectar.

58.description: A colossal, broad-canopied tropical shade tree forming a massive umbrella crown, famous for its delicate pink powderpuff blooms and leaflets that fold up before rain and dusk.
identifyingFeatures: Colossal umbrella-shaped spreading crown often wider (30-40 m) than the tree is tall
Bipinnate compound leaves that fold closed in rainy, overcast weather and at sunset (nyctinasty)
Bicolor fluffy powderpuff flower heads composed of dozens of long stamens, white at base and rosy-pink at tips
Thick, straight or slightly curved blackish-brown seed pods with sweet, sticky pulp inside
58.habitat: Spacious public parks, university campuses, expansive highway avenues, and rural pasture borders.
58.distribution: Native to tropical Central and South America; extensively planted throughout India as a premier canopy shade tree.
uses: Unrivaled urban park shade tree providing cooling canopies covering entire intersections
Sweet, sticky seed pods avidly eaten by cattle, goats, and horses as nutritious fodder
Durable, attractively figured hardwood used for artisan carved bowls and furniture
careTips: Plant only in expansive open parks or wide avenues where massive spreading branches have room to expand
Needs full sun and tolerates diverse soil conditions from moist alluvial to seasonal drought
Prune young trees to establish strong branch unions free of narrow, weak crotches
58.toxicityNote: Non-toxic; sweet pods are safe fodder for animals and safe around humans.
58.funFact: The name 'Rain Tree' comes from the phenomenon of its leaflets folding up before rainfall, allowing raindrops to pass directly through the canopy to the ground beneath.

59.description: A towering, fast-growing evergreen tree with peeling shaggy bark, sickle-shaped aromatic blue-green leaves, and pungent cineole-rich medicinal essential oils.
identifyingFeatures: Tall, straight, smooth trunk with peeling ribbons of grey, cream, and brown bark shedding continuously
Juvenile leaves are broad, silvery-blue and opposite; adult leaves are long, curved, sickle-shaped (falcate) and dark green
Woody, warty, top-shaped capsules (gum nuts) with a four-valved opening releasing tiny seeds
Intensely pungent, sharp camphoraceous cineole aroma when foliage is crushed
59.habitat: Hill stations, timber plantations, farm boundary windbreaks, and drained marshy lowlands.
59.distribution: Native to southeastern Australia; widely planted in India's Nilgiri Hills, Punjab, and agroforestry sectors.
uses: Steam distillation of leaves produces medicinal Nilgiri oil (eucalyptol) for decongestant balms, inhalants, and throat lozenges
Rapidly grown commercial timber for paper pulp, cardboard, utility poles, and construction scaffolding
Planted in waterlogged areas to rapidly lower water tables and help control mosquito breeding
careTips: Requires full direct sunshine and rapid-draining soil; avoid planting near residential foundations or septic systems
Deep, aggressive root system consumes enormous amounts of water; keep away from shallow garden beds
Extremely fire-prone due to volatile resinous leaf oils; maintain cleared firebreaks
59.toxicityNote: TOXIC INGESTION: Concentrated eucalyptus essential oil is TOXIC if swallowed, causing burning in mouth, vomiting, dizziness, seizures, and respiratory failure, particularly in children and household pets. Diluted topical balms and steam inhalations are safe.
59.funFact: The Nilgiri Hills ('Blue Mountains') in Tamil Nadu got their modern blue haze association partly from the vast plantations of blue gum eucalyptus trees introduced there in the mid-19th century.

60.description: The quintessential cereal grass of tropical Asia, cultivated in flooded paddy terraces and alluvial plains to nourish more than half of the human global population.
identifyingFeatures: Erect annual clumping grass with hollow, jointed round culms up to 1-1.8 m tall
Long, flat linear leaf blades with rough scaberulous margins and a prominent membranous ligule
Arching terminal panicles bearing flattened one-flowered spikelets that mature into golden husked grains
60.habitat: Flooded wetland paddies, irrigated river deltas, and terraced hillside water basins.
60.distribution: Native to the Yangtze and Ganges river basins; cultivated across all rice belts of India and Asia.
uses: Staple dietary carbohydrate grain eaten steamed, boiled into khichdi, or ground into idli and dosa batter
Sacred grain (Akshata) used in every Hindu ritual, wedding blessing, and puja offering
Rice straw used for cattle fodder, thatched roofs, mushroom cultivation, and biodegradable paper
careTips: Requires flooded or saturated muddy soil during vegetative tillering and panicle development
Thrives in hot, humid tropical climates with intense uninterrupted sunlight
Drain water from paddy fields 10-14 days before grain harvesting
60.toxicityNote: Non-toxic; raw husks are indigestible and must be milled. Cooked rice is one of the gentlest hypoallergenic foods known.
60.funFact: India is the world's largest exporter of rice, cultivating thousands of fragrant heritage varieties including the legendary long-grain Basmati and aromatic Gobindobhog.

61.description: The world's foremost cool-season temperate cereal grass, bearing dense awned spikes of golden grains that provide the flour foundation for rotis, breads, and pastas.
identifyingFeatures: Upright annual tufted grass with hollow ribbed stems reaching 0.6 to 1.2 m in height
Flat, narrow linear leaves with clasping claw-like auricles at the junction of sheath and blade
Dense, erect terminal compound spikes with zigzag rachis bearing spikelets with or without bristly awns ('beards')
Oval golden-brown caryopsis grain with a deep longitudinal groove along one side
61.habitat: Irrigated winter farmlands, alluvial river plains (Indo-Gangetic plain), and temperate prairies.
61.distribution: Originated in the Fertile Crescent of the Middle East; premier Rabi winter crop of northern India (Punjab, Haryana, UP).
uses: Milled into whole-wheat atta for daily rotis, chapatis, parathas, and refined maida for breads and bakery goods
Wheat straw (bhusa) serves as the primary winter dry livestock fodder across rural north India
Tender green wheatgrass juiced as an antioxidant-rich wellness beverage
careTips: Sown as a winter (Rabi) crop in northern India, requiring cool vegetative temperatures and warm ripening weather
Needs well-drained, fertile alluvial or clay loam soil; cannot tolerate prolonged waterlogging
Requires 4-6 timed crown root irrigations during crucial growth stages
61.toxicityNote: Non-toxic; contains gluten proteins which cause immune reactions in individuals with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.
61.funFact: Common bread wheat is an allohexaploid plant, meaning its complex genome contains six sets of chromosomes derived from three distinct ancestral wild grass species.

62.description: A robust, tall annual giant cereal grass with stout prop roots, broad arching leaves, terminal male tassel flowers, and ears of tightly packed sweet or starchy kernels.
identifyingFeatures: Tall, solid, bamboo-like unbranched erect stalk reaching 2-3 meters in height, supported by stout aerial prop roots at base
Broad, wavy-margined linear leaves clasping the stem on alternating sides
Separate male and female flowers on same plant: terminal branching tassel (male) and axillary ear with silky styles (female)
Cylindrical cobs tightly wrapped in leafy husks, packed with rows of yellow, white, or multicolor grains
62.habitat: Agricultural grain fields, river terraces, and warm temperate-to-tropical croplands.
62.distribution: Domesticated in southern Mexico over 9,000 years ago; now cultivated extensively across India and worldwide.
uses: Fresh ears roasted over charcoal on Indian street carts (bhutta) with lime and black salt
Ground into yellow makki ka atta for iconic winter Makki ki Roti paired with Sarson ka Saag
Major global industrial source of cornstarch, corn syrup, poultry feed, and biofuel ethanol
careTips: Requires full direct sun and rich, nitrogen-heavy, well-aerated soil
Plant in blocks of several short rows rather than single long rows to facilitate wind pollination
Keep consistently watered, particularly when tassels and silk emerge
62.toxicityNote: Non-toxic; corn kernels and silks are completely safe and edible for humans and domestic animals.
62.funFact: Every single strand of silk on an ear of corn connects to a single egg inside, meaning every single kernel on a cob must be individually pollinated by a grain of airborne pollen.

63.description: A gigantic, thick-stemmed perennial clumping grass with stout, jointed, fibrous stalks brimming with sweet sucrose-rich juice, grown as the world's primary sugar source.
identifyingFeatures: Massive clumping stalks (culms) 3 to 5 meters tall and 3 to 5 cm thick, ringed with noticeable nodes
Stalks colored green, yellow, purple, or deep burgundy with sweet, fibrous, juice-saturated inner pith
Long, narrow, sword-like linear leaves with sharp serrulate edges and a pale prominent central midrib
Large, feathery, plume-like silvery-white terminal panicle known as an 'arrow'
63.habitat: Tropical and subtropical alluvial plains with high water availability and intense warmth.
63.distribution: Native to New Guinea and Southeast Asia; historically refined in India where crystalline sugar was invented.
uses: Stalks freshly crushed on Indian street stalls for refreshing sugarcane juice (Ganne ka ras) flavored with ginger and mint
Boiled and concentrated into traditional unrefined jaggery (gur) and refined crystalline table sugar
Bagasse fiber burned for thermal co-generation energy and molasses fermented into industrial ethanol
careTips: Requires 10-12 months of hot tropical weather, high humidity, and copious irrigation
Prefers deep, rich, fertile loam or heavy clay soils with good drainage
Propagated vegetatively via stem cuttings ('setts') bearing at least 2-3 healthy eye buds
63.toxicityNote: Completely non-toxic; cane juice and jaggery are safe foods; moldy red-rot sugarcane should be avoided.
63.funFact: India was the first country in the world to invent the process of crystallizing sugarcane juice into solid crystals (Sanskrit: 'Khanda', origin of the English word 'candy') over 2,500 years ago.

64.description: An evergreen glossy-leaved shrub pruned into flat-topped bushes across rolling misty hills, whose tender young bud flushes yield black, green, oolong, and white teas.
identifyingFeatures: Pruned flat-topped evergreen bushes (plucking tables) with dense, woody branching
Alternate, elliptic-to-lanceolate leathery glossy leaves with serrated margins and silky hairs on young flushes
Small, nodding, fragrant creamy-white flowers with 7-8 petals and a prominent cluster of bright yellow stamens
Three-lobed woody green-to-brown capsules containing round brown oily seeds
64.habitat: Misty subtropical mountain slopes, cool elevated plateaus, and acidic highland hill stations.
64.distribution: Native to East Asia and the Assam Brahmaputra valley of Northeast India; grown across Darjeeling, Assam, and Nilgiris.
uses: Harvesting 'two leaves and a bud' processed into world-renowned Darjeeling, Assam, and Nilgiri teas
Brewed as daily Indian spiced milk tea (Masala Chai) boiled with cardamom, ginger, and cloves
Rich in polyphenol antioxidants (EGCG), theanine, and gentle caffeine for mental clarity
careTips: Requires strongly acidic, well-draining soil (pH 4.5 to 5.5) rich in organic humus
Thrives under high rainfall, cool temperatures, and frequent misty humidity with morning sun
Requires regular plucking and pruning to maintain a dense vegetative flushing canopy
64.toxicityNote: Completely safe as a standard beverage. Highly concentrated botanical dietary supplements containing isolated epigallocatechin gallate (EGCG) can cause rare idiosyncratic hepatotoxicity; caffeine and theophylline content makes tea toxic to dogs and cats.
64.funFact: All true teas — black, green, white, oolong, and pu-erh — come from the very same botanical species, Camellia sinensis; the dramatic differences in flavor and color arise solely from how the leaves are oxidized and processed.

sources.name: ASPCA Animal Poison Control & EFSA Scientific Opinion on Green Tea Catechins

65.description: A branching subtropical shrub bearing cream-to-pink mallow flowers, lobed leaves, and leathery green bolls that burst open at maturity to reveal snowy clouds of soft cellulose lint.
identifyingFeatures: Erect, branching herbaceous shrub reaching 1 to 1.5 m with reddish hairy stems
Broad, palmately 3-to-5 lobed cordate leaves with hairy undersides and dark gland dots
Large, cup-shaped creamy-white or pale yellow flowers that turn dull pinkish-purple on the second day
Ovoid pointed green bolls that split into 3-5 valves, revealing fluffy white fibrous lint enclosing dark seeds
65.habitat: Warm, sunny agricultural river plains, black cotton soil tracts (Regur soils), and semi-arid valleys.
65.distribution: Native to Central America; widely cultivated throughout western and central India (Gujarat, Maharashtra, Telangana).
uses: World's most important natural textile fiber ('white gold') woven into breathable cotton garments, towels, and bedsheets
Cottonseed crushed to extract edible cottonseed oil and high-protein livestock meal cake (khal)
Absorbent medical cotton wool used universally in wound dressings and surgical care
careTips: Requires deep, moisture-retentive black basaltic soils (Regur) or fertile alluvial loam
Needs hot weather, full sun, and at least 180 to 200 frost-free sunny days
Keep dry and warm during boll bursting and lint harvesting to preserve fiber quality
65.toxicityNote: Purified fiber and refined cottonseed oil are safe. Raw unrefined cottonseed and foliage contain the toxic polyphenolic pigment gossypol, which causes severe myocardial necrosis, pulmonary edema, and male sterility in monogastric animals and humans
65.funFact: Cotton fibers are practically pure natural cellulose (over 90%), arranged in hollow microscopic spirals that make them exceptionally soft, absorbent, and breathable.

66.description: A cool-season annual agricultural herb that carpets winter fields in sea of radiant canary-yellow 4-petaled blossoms, yielding pungent leaves and fiery oil-rich seeds.
identifyingFeatures: Erect, smooth glaucous branching green stem up to 1-1.5 meters tall
Lower leaves are large, lyrate-pinnatifid with scalloped margins; upper leaves are smaller, lanceolate and sub-entire
Abundant terminal racemes of bright golden-yellow cruciform (4-petaled cross-shaped) flowers
Slender, cylindrical ascending silique pods (beaked pods) containing rows of tiny spherical reddish-brown seeds
66.habitat: Winter agricultural fields, alluvial riverbanks, and fertile northern plains.
66.distribution: Native to Central Asia and the Indian subcontinent; iconic winter crop of Punjab, Rajasthan, Haryana, and Bengal.
uses: Pungent brown seeds cold-pressed into Kacchi Ghani mustard oil, the signature cooking oil of North and Eastern India
Tender winter leaves boiled and slow-simmered into Sarson ka Saag served with Makki ki Roti
Seeds ground into zesty kasundi and fish-curry pastes (Shorshe Ilish) in Bengal
careTips: Grown as a winter Rabi crop; thrives in cool weather and full direct sunlight
Prefers well-drained loamy soil; sensitive to water stagnation during early root development
Harvest seed pods when plants turn golden-brown before pods shatter open
66.toxicityNote: Non-toxic in normal culinary use; mustard oil contains erucic acid and allyl isothiocyanate which gives it a pungent sharp bite. Safe and widely consumed.
66.funFact: The characteristic pungent nasal heat of mustard is only released when seeds or leaves are crushed in water, which activates the myrosinase enzyme to produce allyl isothiocyanate.

67.description: A sprawling, gland-dotted annual herb with aromatic dissected leaves, yellow star-shaped blossoms, and juicy red berries that are a cornerstone of modern world gastronomy.
identifyingFeatures: Sprawling, glandular-pubescent weak stems covered in sticky hairs that release a strong, pungent odor
Pinnately divided leaves with irregular ovate, serrated leaflets
Clusters of nodding, star-shaped yellow flowers with reflexed petals and a conical yellow anther cone
Fleshy, juicy globose-to-oblong berries ripening from firm green to brilliant scarlet-red with multiple seed locules
67.habitat: Kitchen gardens, commercial vegetable farm plots, polyhouses, and terrace containers.
67.distribution: Native to western South America (Andes); now grown universally across India and worldwide.
uses: Essential savory flavor base for Indian gravies, curries, rasams, and fresh kachumber salads
Richest dietary source of the potent antioxidant carotenoid lycopene, supporting cardiovascular health
Processed commercially into tomato puree, ketchups, and canned sauces
careTips: Requires at least 6-8 hours of direct sunshine and support trellising or tomato cages
Water deeply and consistently at the soil level; irregular watering causes blossom end rot and fruit splitting
Pinch out side-suckers from leaf axils on indeterminate varieties to focus energy on fruit ripening
67.toxicityNote: RIPE FRUIT IS SAFE AND EDIBLE. FOLIAGE AND GREEN UNRIPE FRUITS ARE TOXIC: Leaves, stems, and unripened green tomatoes contain toxic glycoalkaloids (solanine and tomatine). Ingestion of green plant parts can cause abdominal pain, vomiting, and diarrhea in humans and pets.
67.funFact: Botanically, the tomato is a true berry, but a famous 1893 US Supreme Court case (Nix v. Hedden) legally classified it as a vegetable for taxation purposes because it is eaten as part of the main meal.

68.description: A bushy herbaceous plant producing solitary white star flowers and glossy elongated pods containing spicy capsaicin that gives heat and fire to Indian cuisine.
identifyingFeatures: Bushy, angular-stemmed compact plant reaching 0.5 to 1 meter in height
Alternate, smooth, ovate-to-lanceolate leaves with entire margins and pointed tips
Solitary, nodding white or greenish-white star-like flowers borne in leaf axils
Glossy, elongated pendant or erect berries ripening from green to fiery crimson-red, packed with heat on placental membranes
68.habitat: Agricultural vegetable farms, sunny home gardens, and raised garden containers.
68.distribution: Native to Mesoamerica; introduced to India by Portuguese traders in the 16th century, now an inseparable national staple.
uses: Indispensable spice added fresh (hari mirch) or sun-dried and powdered (lal mirch) to almost all savory Indian dishes
Reported in traditional and modern herbal literature; standardized topical capsaicin preparations are used for temporary soothing of joint and muscular discomfort
Traditional Indian protective amulets (nimbu-mirchi) hung to ward off the evil eye (nazar)
careTips: Thrives in hot, sunny conditions with rich, well-draining garden soil
Water moderately; slightly restricting water during fruiting actually increases capsaicin heat intensity
Apply high-potash fertilizer when flower buds initiate
68.toxicityNote: Fruit is culinary safe; capsaicin is an intense mucous membrane irritant. Wash hands thoroughly after chopping; avoid touching eyes. Excessive intake can cause gastric pain. Keep away from household pets.
68.funFact: The fiery heat in chillies is measured on the Scoville Heat Scale; capsaicin does not cause an actual physical burn, but tricks sensory nerve endings into signaling extreme heat to the brain.

69.description: A robust, bushy annual vegetable herb bearing starry violet flowers and large, glossy, deep-purple fleshy berries beloved across India for hearty, tender roasted and curried dishes.
identifyingFeatures: Bushy, coarse erect stem up to 1-1.5 m, sometimes armed with sharp prickles on calyx and stem
Large, alternate, coarsely lobed dull grey-green leaves covered in soft downy star-shaped hairs
Star-shaped violet or purple flowers with yellow central stamens clustered in leaf axils
Large, glossy, pear-shaped or globular berries with a persistent spiny green calyx and tender spongy white seed-flecked flesh
69.habitat: Fertile alluvial plains, homestead vegetable plots, and sunny agricultural farmlands.
69.distribution: Native to the Indian subcontinent and Southeast Asia; cultivated across India since pre-Vedic antiquity.
uses: Charred and mashed over open flame to create the iconic smoky Baingan Bharta
Deep-fried in spiced gram-flour batter for Bengali Beguni, or stuffed in Maharashtrian Bharli Vangi
Excellent source of dietary fiber, nasunin anthocyanins in purple skin, and copper
careTips: Requires hot, sunny weather and deep, fertile, organically rich loam soil
Stake heavy fruiting branches to keep heavy eggplants off wet soil
Harvest fruits while skin remains glossy; dull skin indicates overripe bitter seeds
69.toxicityNote: Cooked fruit is safe and nutritious. RAW FOLIAGE AND STEMS ARE TOXIC: Leaves and raw unripened fruit contain the toxic glycoalkaloid solanine; do not consume raw green parts or allow pets to chew foliage.
69.funFact: Botanical and linguistic records confirm that brinjal was domesticated in India over 4,000 years ago, and Sanskrit literature documents over 30 distinct historical culinary varieties.

70.description: A tall, erect warm-season annual herb with hibiscus-like pale yellow flowers and elongated ridged green seed pods prized for their tender texture and natural mucilaginous thickening.
identifyingFeatures: Stout, erect semi-woody hairy stem growing 1 to 2 meters tall
Broad, palmately 5-to-7 lobed leaves with coarse serrated edges on long petioles
Showy, creamy-yellow hibiscus-like flowers with a deep dark-maroon or purple throat center
Elongated, ridged, tapering green pyramidal capsules filled with round white seeds and rich mucilage
70.habitat: Summer agricultural vegetable beds, warm alluvial loam fields, and kitchen gardens.
70.distribution: Native to tropical Africa and South Asia; enthusiastically cultivated as a daily staple vegetable across India.
uses: Staple Indian vegetable dish: dry-spiced stir-fry Bhindi Masala, Kurkuri Bhindi, or Bengali Dherosh Chorchori
Natural mucilage used as a thickener in traditional southern gumbos and stews
High natural source of soluble dietary fiber, Vitamin K, and folate
careTips: Thrives in hot summer sunshine; seeds fail to germinate in cold or waterlogged soil
Plant in rich, well-draining garden soil enriched with mature compost
Harvest pods every 2-3 days while they are tender and snap easily; old pods become tough and stringy
70.toxicityNote: Completely non-toxic; pods, leaves, and seeds are edible and safe for humans and animals.
70.funFact: India is the world's undisputed king of okra production, harvesting over 60% of the entire global commercial okra crop each year.

71.description: The world's premier tuber crop, a sprawling nightshade family herb bearing starchy underground stem tubers that form the backbone of Indian street food and global cooking.
identifyingFeatures: Sprawling herbaceous green stems with pinnately compound leaves composed of ovate leaflets
Clusters of white, pink, or pale lavender star-shaped flowers with bright yellow protruding anthers
Small, green tomato-like seed balls (berries) borne above ground containing true botanical seeds
Starchy underground stem tubers with protective corky skins and spirally arranged buds ('eyes')
71.habitat: Cool-season agricultural plains (Indo-Gangetic plain), temperate mountain slopes, and sandy loam beds.
71.distribution: Native to the South American Andes; introduced to India in the 17th century, now grown everywhere from UP to Bengal.
uses: Heart of Indian comfort cuisine: Aloo Gobi, Aloo Paratha, Samosa stuffing, Dum Aloo, and street chaat
Rich source of digestible dietary carbohydrates, potassium, and Vitamin B6
Commercial production of potato starch, flour, and snack chips
careTips: Grown as a cool winter crop in the plains, or summer crop in the Himalayan hills
Requires loose, deeply tilled sandy loam soil to allow unhindered tuber expansion
Hill soil up around growing stems regularly to protect swelling tubers from sunlight exposure
71.toxicityNote: TUBERS ARE SAFE WHEN SOUND. GREEN PARTS AND SPROUTS ARE TOXIC: Green sun-exposed potato peel, green tubers, sprouts, and all aboveground foliage contain poisonous solanine and chaconine glycoalkaloids. Ingestion causes nausea, vomiting, abdominal cramping, and headaches. NEVER eat green potatoes.
71.funFact: Potatoes are underground modified stems (tubers), not roots; the 'eyes' of a potato are actually dormant axillary buds capable of sprouting into new clonal plants.

72.description: A biennial pungent bulb herb with hollow cylindrical leaves, globose spherical umbels of starry white flowers, and layered fleshy underground bulbs indispensable in world cooking.
identifyingFeatures: Hollow, cylindrical, glaucous bluish-green leaves growing in a fan from the underground basal stem plate
Layered underground bulb composed of concentric fleshy modified leaf bases enclosed in dry, papery brown-to-purple tunics
Tall, hollow flowering scape topped by a dense spherical umbel of small white or pale greenish flowers
Strong, pungent lachrymatory aroma released when bulb cells are ruptured or sliced
72.habitat: Agricultural crop fields, market vegetable gardens, and alluvial vegetable terraces.
72.distribution: Native to Central/Southwestern Asia; grown in colossal quantities across Maharashtra (Nashik), Gujarat, and nationwide.
uses: Fundamental aromatic flavor foundation for Indian tadkas, gravies, biryanis, and salads
High natural source of quercetin, a powerful antioxidant flavonoid supporting cellular health

Folk remedy for hair thinning; a pilot clinical trial showed crude topical onion juice promoted hair regrowth in patchy alopecia areata due to high sulfur and flavonoid content, though further large-scale validation is needed
careTips: Needs full direct sun and fertile, loose, sandy loam soil free of rocks
Keep soil weed-free and uniformly moist during early bulb swelling; withhold water as tops flop over
Allow harvested bulbs to dry and cure in a well-ventilated shaded space for several weeks
72.toxicityNote: SAFE FOR HUMANS. TOXIC TO PETS: Contains organosulfoxides and N-propyl disulfide that are highly toxic to dogs, cats, and horses, destroying red blood cells and triggering life-threatening hemolytic anemia.
72.funFact: Onions make you cry because slicing cell walls mixes sulfenic acids with enzymes to create syn-propanethial-S-oxide gas, which reacts with tear-duct moisture to form mild sulfuric acid.

73.description: A feathery, aromatic annual herb whose refreshing citrus-herbal leaves (cilantro) and warm, spicy-citrus dried spherical seeds (coriander) are central to Indian cookery.
identifyingFeatures: Slender, erect hollow branching stems up to 30-60 cm tall
Dimorphic foliage: broad, fan-lobed lower leaves and finely dissected feathery upper leaves
Compound umbels of tiny white to pale pinkish asymmetric flowers
Globose, ribbed, hollow dual-seeded schizocarps turning from green to fragrant straw-brown
73.habitat: Sunny vegetable beds, alluvial winter croplands, and kitchen herb pots.
73.distribution: Native to the Mediterranean and southwestern Asia; widely cultivated in Rajasthan, Gujarat, and across India.
uses: Fresh chopped leaves (cilantro / green dhaniya) used as the universal finishing garnish on all Indian curries and dals
Dry roasted seeds ground into dhaniya powder, a foundational warm spice in garam masala and curry powders

Classical Ayurvedic cold infusion of crushed seeds (Dhaniya hima) is recognized by the European Medicines Agency as a traditional herbal medicine for symptomatic relief of mild spasmodic gastrointestinal complaints
careTips: Thrives in cool weather and morning sun; rapidly bolts to flower in hot, dry conditions
Keep soil evenly moist using well-aerated, fertile potting loam
Sow successive seeds every 3 weeks for an uninterrupted supply of fresh tender leaves
73.toxicityNote: Non-toxic and edible; a harmless genetic variation in OR6A2 olfactory receptor genes causes cilantro to taste intensely like soap to about 10-15% of people.
73.funFact: Every part of the coriander plant is edible — the tender leafy greens (cilantro), the flowers, the dried seeds (coriander), and even the pungent roots which form the base of Thai curry pastes.

74.description: A cool-season leafy annual vegetable forming basal rosettes of succulent, deep-green tender leaves celebrated worldwide for their rich iron, folate, and vitamin content.
identifyingFeatures: Basal rosette of succulent, deep-green, ovate to triangular-hastate leaves with prominent veins
Leaves can be smooth-flat or deeply crinkled (savoy)
Dioecious flowering (male and female flowers on separate plants) producing tiny greenish apetalous clusters on upright spikes
Compact cluster of small hard, spiny or smooth fruits enclosing seeds
74.habitat: Cool-season vegetable plots, raised kitchen garden beds, and fertile agricultural loams.
74.distribution: Native to ancient Persia (central and western Asia); universally cultivated across India as a premier winter leafy green.
uses: Blanched and pureed with paneer into the beloved restaurant classic Palak Paneer
Stir-fried with potatoes in Aloo Palak or simmered into comforting Bengali Palang Shaker Ghonto
Rich in lutein, zeaxanthin, iron, folate, and Vitamins A, C, and K
careTips: Requires cool temperatures (10-22°C); hot weather immediately triggers bitter flowering stalks (bolting)
Provide full winter sun and nitrogen-rich, moisture-retentive, well-draining garden soil
Harvest outer leaves continuously (cut-and-come-again) to prolong the vegetative harvest window
74.toxicityNote: Wholesome and nutrient-dense in dietary amounts. High concentrations of soluble oxalic acid can bind dietary minerals and dramatically increase urinary oxalate excretion, posing a significant risk of calcium oxalate urolithiasis in susceptible individuals
74.funFact: The famous myth that spinach contains astronomical amounts of iron originated from a 19th-century German chemist who misplaced a decimal point, attributing tenfold the actual iron content to the leaf.

75.description: A vigorous annual climbing vine with soft hairy leaves, nocturnal white flowers, and smooth pale-green cylindrical or bottle-shaped fruits prized for cooling summer dishes.
identifyingFeatures: Vigorous twining tendril-bearing vine with soft, velvet-hairy musk-scented stems
Broad, heart-shaped (cordate) or kidney-shaped leaves with shallow lobes and wavy margins
Solitary, nocturnal white flowers with crinkled petals opening late afternoon
Smooth, pale-green fruits in cylindrical, club, or dumbbell shapes with white spongy flesh and flat seeds
75.habitat: Alluvial agricultural fields, village roof trellises, and home garden pergolas.
75.distribution: Native to tropical Africa and South Asia; cultivated throughout India for thousands of years.
uses: Light, cooling staple vegetable cooked into Lauki ki Sabzi, Lauki Kofta, Lauki Kheer, and Bengali Lau Ghonto

Fresh sweet bottle gourd juice is traditionally consumed as a cooling digestive beverage; however, bitter juice contains lethal cucurbitacins and must never be consumed. Discard immediately if any bitter taste is detected
Dried, hollowed woody gourds historically crafted into the soundbox resonator of the sitar, tanpura, and rudra veena
careTips: Provide a sturdy bamboo arbor, trellis, or rooftop scaffolding to support heavy hanging gourds
Requires full direct sunshine and organically enriched, moisture-retentive loam soil
Water generously and consistently during vine growth and fruit swelling
75.toxicityNote: CRITICAL TOXICITY WARNING: SWEET GOURD IS SAFE; BITTER BOTTLE GOURD IS DEADLY POISONOUS. Never consume bottle gourd juice that tastes bitter. Bitter gourds contain lethal concentrations of toxic cucurbitacins B and D, triggering severe toxic shock, upper gastrointestinal hemorrhage (hematemesis), necrotizing pancreatitis, and organ failure. The Indian Council of Medical Research (ICMR) mandates tasting a small raw piece before juicing or cooking; discard immediately if bitter
75.funFact: Dried, hollowed bottle gourds were among the world's very first domesticated containers and floating water jugs, carried across oceans by early human navigators over 10,000 years ago.

76.description: A vigorous creeping or climbing vine with large mottled leaves, bright golden-orange bell-shaped blossoms, and heavy ribbed fruits with nutrient-dense, sweet orange flesh.
identifyingFeatures: Extensive trailing or climbing vine with angled stems and branched tendrils
Large, soft, dark green heart-shaped leaves often patterned with silver-white blotches at vein intersections
Large, showy bright yellow-orange flared trumpet flowers (edible blossoms)
Large variable fruit (globose, flattened, or oblong) with ribbed rind and thick, sweet orange flesh enclosing flat seeds
76.habitat: Farmland fields, river sandbanks (diara farming), and home compost beds.
76.distribution: Native to Mesoamerica and South America; universally cultivated throughout India as a staple vegetable.
uses: Cooked into sweet-and-sour Kaddu ki Sabzi, Bengali Kumror Chhokka, and sambar stews
Nutrient-dense seeds (magaz) roasted as healthy snacks or ground into festive sweet gravies
Rich dietary source of beta-carotene (provitamin A), lutein, and potassium
careTips: Requires vast ground area or heavy-duty arbors to support rambling 5-10 meter vines
Thrives in hot, sunny weather and loose, fertile soil enriched with aged cow manure
Mulch soil beneath developing fruits with straw to prevent rot from ground moisture
76.toxicityNote: Non-toxic; flesh, blossoms, tender leaves, and seeds are completely edible and safe for humans and pets.
76.funFact: In Bengali cuisine, practically zero waste is generated from pumpkin: the flesh, tender climbing shoot tips (kumro shaak), yellow flowers (kumro phul bhaja), and seeds are all prized delicacies.

77.description: A fast-growing rough-stemmed annual climbing vine bearing small yellow flowers and crisp, cooling cylindrical green fruits containing over 95% water.
identifyingFeatures: Slender climbing or trailing vine with rough bristly stems and unbranched coiled tendrils
Rough, triangular-ovate palmately 3-5 lobed leaves with acute lobes
Small yellow star-like flowers in leaf axils (separate male and female flowers)
Elongated cylindrical green fruits with warty or smooth skin and pale crisp seed-filled juicy flesh
77.habitat: Riverbed sands, alluvial vegetable farms, polyhouses, and home garden trellises.
77.distribution: Native to the foothills of the Himalayas in India; cultivated across the world for over 3,000 years.
uses: Essential cooling raw salad vegetable eaten fresh with lemon juice and chaat masala, or folded into boondi raita
Natural hydrator containing over 95% water, electrolytes, and silica
Chilled slices placed over eyes to reduce puffiness and soothe tired skin
careTips: Trellis vines vertically to keep cucumbers clean, straight, and well-aerated
Requires consistent, deep watering; moisture stress produces bitter, misshapen fruits
Harvest cucumbers while crisp and firm before seeds enlarge and skins turn yellow
77.toxicityNote: Safe and wholesome; occasional bitter cucumbers contain elevated cucurbitacins (usually concentrated near the stem end) and should be trimmed or discarded.
77.funFact: Ancient Sanskrit texts mention cucumber cultivation under the name 'Trapusha' over three millennia ago, confirming India as the original botanical homeland of the global cucumber.

78.description: A low-growing legume herb renowned for its remarkable habit of geocarpy, where pollinated flower stems bend downward and drill beneath the soil to develop underground pods.
identifyingFeatures: Low, bushy, or sprawling annual legume reaching 30-50 cm in height
Pinnate leaves with four broad, obovate leaflets arranged in two opposite pairs
Bright yellow pea-like flowers blooming low on stems; after pollination, the floral stalk ('peg') elongates downward and burrows into the soil
Reticulated woody underground pods containing 1 to 4 oil-rich edible seeds covered in thin reddish-brown papery seed coats
78.habitat: Sandy loam agricultural plains, light well-drained soils, and semi-arid cropping belts.
78.distribution: Native to South America; extensively cultivated across western and southern India (Gujarat, Andhra Pradesh, Tamil Nadu).
uses: Roasted, salted, or boiled as iconic winter street snacks (moongphali) across Indian railway stations and markets
Major commercial source of groundnut oil, the preferred traditional cooking oil of Gujarat and Maharashtra
High natural source of plant protein, healthy monounsaturated fats, resveratrol, and Vitamin E
careTips: Requires light, loose, sandy loam soil so emerging pegs can easily penetrate underground
Thrives in warm, sunny weather; sensitive to soil compaction and waterlogging
Keep soil loose around the base of plants during flowering and pegging stages
78.toxicityNote: Non-toxic; peanuts are one of the most common severe food allergens, capable of triggering life-threatening anaphylaxis in allergic individuals. Ensure peanuts are stored dry to avoid toxic aflatoxin mold.
78.funFact: Peanuts are not true nuts at all, but botanical legumes related to peas and beans, famous for their unique habit of flowering in the air and ripening their pods underground.

79.description: A tall, erect annual bast-fiber herb celebrated as the source of 'The Golden Fiber', with slender stalks that yield strong, silky, biodegradable natural fibers after retting.
identifyingFeatures: Tall, straight, slender unbranched annual herb reaching 2 to 4 meters in height
Alternate, ovate-to-lanceolate leaves with serrated margins, characterized by two hair-like tail bristles at the base of the blade
Small, bright yellow 5-petaled flowers borne solitary or in pairs in leaf axils
Elongated, ribbed cylindrical 10-angled seed capsules containing numerous small grayish seeds
79.habitat: Alluvial floodplains, water-rich river basins, and monsoon-inundated delta soils.
79.distribution: Native to the Indian subcontinent and tropical Africa; Bengal (India and Bangladesh) is the global epicentre of jute production.
uses: Bast fibers woven into burlap, gunny sacks, twine, eco-friendly shopping bags, and geo-textiles ('The Golden Fiber')
Tender mucilaginous young leaves cooked as a prized nutritious green potherb (Pat shaak) in Bengal and Egypt (Molokhia)
Completely biodegradable, eco-friendly alternative to synthetic plastic packaging materials
careTips: Requires high temperatures, high monsoon humidity, and deep, standing alluvial silt soils
Grown during the monsoon season when rainfall is abundant
Retting: harvested stalks must be submerged in slow-flowing fresh water for 2-3 weeks to soften and strip fibers
79.toxicityNote: Tender young leaves are a popular, safe, edible green vegetable (Molokhia). Mature seed capsules contain potent cardenolide cardiac glycosides (olitoriside, corchoroside A) that induce digitalis-like cardiac toxicity and must never be consumed
79.funFact: Jute is the second most important natural vegetable fiber in the world after cotton, and is celebrated as 'The Golden Fiber' for its natural golden sheen and vital economic importance.

80.description: An evergreen climbing tropical vine ubiquitously grown in Indian households in jars of water and hanging baskets, prized for its glossy heart-shaped variegated leaves and feng shui prosperity symbolism.
identifyingFeatures: Trailing or climbing vine with adventitious aerial roots that grip supports or flourish directly in standing water
Glossy, heart-shaped (cordate) juvenile leaves marbled with vibrant splashes of yellow, cream, or lime-green
In wild mature forest conditions, leaves become gigantic (up to 1 m long) with deep pinnatifid leaf splits
Almost never flowers in domestic cultivation due to a genetic deficiency in gibberellin synthesis
80.habitat: Indoor living rooms, balconies, office corridors, and tropical tree trunks.
80.distribution: Native to Mo'orea in French Polynesia; universally cultivated across India and worldwide as an indestructible houseplant.
uses: Popular Vastu Shastra and Feng Shui houseplant believed to attract wealth, prosperity, and positive energy
Top-rated indoor air-purifying plant shown to remove indoor toxins including formaldehyde, benzene, and xylene
Versatile ornamental grown in soil pots, moss poles, or simple glass bottles filled with water
careTips: Thrives in bright indirect light; tolerates low-light conditions (though variegation fades in deep shade)
Allow the top 2 inches of soil to dry out between waterings; avoid soggy, anaerobic soil
If growing in water jars, change the water every 7-10 days to maintain oxygenation and prevent algae
80.toxicityNote: TOXIC TO PETS AND CHILDREN: Contains insoluble needle-shaped calcium oxalate crystals (raphides). Chewing any part causes immediate intense burning and stinging of the mouth, tongue, and lips, excessive drooling, difficulty swallowing, and vomiting in cats, dogs, and humans.
80.funFact: Golden Pothos earned the nickname 'Devil's Ivy' because it is nearly impossible to kill and stays vibrantly green even when neglected in windowless dark corners.

81.description: An architectural, virtually indestructible succulent herb with erect, sword-like stiff leaves banded with wavy grey-green horizontal patterns and golden borders.
identifyingFeatures: Dense basal clusters of rigid, erect, vertical sword-shaped succulent leaves growing 0.5 to 1.5 m tall
Distinctive horizontal wavy zigzag banding of light and dark olive-green resembling snakeskin, often with bright yellow margins
Tough, fibrous underground rhizomes that creep and push up new pups
Slender spikes of greenish-white tubular nocturnal flowers emitting a light sweet fragrance in mature plants
81.habitat: Dry tropical rocky forests, shaded arid bushlands, and modern indoor living spaces.
81.distribution: Native to tropical West Africa; grown everywhere globally and across India as a durable indoor plant.
uses: Renowned NASA Clean Air Study plant that converts CO2 into oxygen at night via Crassulacean Acid Metabolism (CAM)
Filters airborne toxins including benzene, formaldehyde, trichloroethylene, and xylene
Architectural focal point for modern minimalist interior design and drought-tolerant rock gardens
careTips: Water sparingly; allow soil to dry out completely between waterings; overwatering causes fatal root rot
Tolerates full blazing sun as well as low-light indoor corners
Use well-aerated cactus or succulent potting soil with perlite and pumice
81.toxicityNote: MILD-TO-MODERATE TOXICITY: Foliage contains saponins. Ingestion by cats and dogs causes excessive salivation, vomiting, nausea, diarrhea, and lethargy.
81.funFact: Unlike most houseplants that release oxygen only during daytime photosynthesis, the Snake Plant performs CAM photosynthesis, releasing oxygen throughout the night, making it ideal for bedrooms.

82.description: A graceful, easy-care clump-forming indoor perennial with arching ribbon-like variegated leaves and long wiry runners bearing miniature plantlets ('spiderettes').
identifyingFeatures: Dense rosette of arching, linear, ribbon-like leaves up to 30-45 cm long, striped with green and creamy-white margins or centers
Long, wiry, yellowish arching stolons (runners) extending 60-90 cm outward
Small, starry, six-petaled white flowers borne along the runners
Miniature tufted plantlets with nascent aerial rootlets dangling from runners like spiders on a web
82.habitat: Coastal riverine forests, rocky forest floors, and residential hanging baskets.
82.distribution: Native to tropical and southern Africa; widely popular throughout India as a hanging terrace and indoor basket plant.
uses: Classic hanging basket and shelf ornamental with cascading tiers of dangling plantlets
Highly effective natural air purifier removing carbon monoxide, formaldehyde, and airborne dust particles
Safe, non-toxic pet-friendly indoor houseplant
careTips: Provide bright, indirect sunlight; direct midday sun scorches and bleaches the tender ribbon leaves
Keep soil evenly moist in spring and summer; water when top inch of soil feels dry
Snip off dangling spiderettes and root them in moist soil or water for effortless propagation
82.toxicityNote: NON-TOXIC: Completely safe for cats, dogs, and children. Cats are often attracted to spider plants because they contain mild compounds with a mild hallucinogenic/catnip-like effect on felines, though it is physically harmless.
82.funFact: A single healthy mother Spider Plant can produce dozens of dangling baby plantlets simultaneously on its arching stolons, giving rise to its common name 'Hen and Chickens'.

83.description: An iconic tropical climbing hemiepiphyte renowned for its enormous, glossy, perforated and deeply split emerald-green leaves and stout aerial cord roots.
identifyingFeatures: Massive climbing vine with stout stems producing thick, cord-like brownish aerial roots
Huge, glossy, heart-shaped leathery leaves that develop dramatic natural perforations (fenestrations) and deep splits
Creamy-white boat-shaped spathe enclosing a stout spadix that develops into an edible cob-like fruit
Fruit covered in hexagonal green scales that pop off naturally when fully ripe to reveal sweet pineapple-banana pulp
83.habitat: Tropical rainforest understory, climbing up mature host trees, and stylish interior spaces.
83.distribution: Native to tropical rainforests of southern Mexico to Panama; massively popular across India as a premium indoor statement plant.
uses: Premier architectural statement plant featured in contemporary interior design and boutique hotels
Naturally removes indoor airborne pollutants and enriches ambient room humidity
Ripe fruit (ceriman) is eaten as a rare delicacy tasting of a hybrid between pineapple, banana, and mango
careTips: Place in bright indirect or filtered sunlight; harsh direct sun bleaches and burns the glossy leaves
Provide a sturdy moss pole, coir totem, or trellis for aerial roots to climb
Water thoroughly when the top 2-3 inches of soil dry; wipe dust off broad leaves with a damp cloth
83.toxicityNote: FOLIAGE AND UNRIPE FRUIT ARE TOXIC: All vegetative parts contain sharp needle-like insoluble calcium oxalate crystals (raphides). Chewing foliage causes intense oral burning, swelling of tongue and throat, and digestive distress in pets and humans. Only the completely ripe fruit (whose outer green scales fall off voluntarily) is edible.
83.funFact: The natural holes in Monstera leaves are called 'fenestrations' (from the Latin for window); they allow hurricane winds to pass through without tearing the leaf and let sunlight filter down to lower foliage.

84.description: An elegant, shade-tolerant evergreen perennial herb with glossy lanceolate leaves and striking, pure-white hood-like floral spathes that resemble white flags of peace.
identifyingFeatures: Dense, stemless clumps of arching, glossy dark green elliptic leaves with sunken veins
Pure snow-white, petal-like oval spathes emerging above the foliage on slender erect stalks
Central, creamy-yellow cylindrical spadix covered in tiny true flowers
Dramatic wilting behavior ('fainting') when thirsty, followed by rapid full recovery within hours of watering
84.habitat: Dense tropical rainforest understory floors, shaded riverbanks, and dimly lit home interiors.
84.distribution: Native to tropical rainforests of Central and South America; universally cultivated as an indoor decorative houseplant.
uses: Celebrated as a symbol of peace, purity, and healing, frequently gifted during housewarmings and milestones
One of the top-performing houseplants for removing benzene, formaldehyde, carbon monoxide, and toluene from indoor air
Thrives in low-light indoor spaces where few other flowering plants can survive
careTips: Prefers medium to low indirect light; direct sunshine will scorch the leaves and brown the white spathes
Keep potting soil consistently moist but never soggy; water as soon as leaves begin to gently droop
Wipe broad leaves periodically to remove dust and maintain high photosynthetic efficiency
84.toxicityNote: TOXIC TO DOGS AND CATS: Contains insoluble calcium oxalate crystals. Ingestion causes immediate oral pain, burning of lips and tongue, drooling, difficulty swallowing, and vomiting. Keep out of reach of domestic pets.
84.funFact: The white 'flower' of the Peace Lily is not a true flower at all, but a modified leaf called a spathe that serves as a protective hood and billboard to guide pollinators to the tiny true flowers on the spadix.

85.description: A magnificent banyan-group evergreen tree native to Northeast India, famous for its colossal buttressed roots, living root bridges of Meghalaya, and thick, glossy, leathery oval leaves.
identifyingFeatures: Massive forest tree developing vast buttresses and aerial prop roots in humid wild habitats
Large, thick, leathery, glossy oblong-oval leaves up to 20-35 cm long with a prominent pinkish-red midrib
Emerging new leaves tightly enclosed in a bright crimson-red or pinkish stipular sheath that drops as the leaf unfurls
Copious thick milky white latex sap exuding immediately from any broken leaf or stem
85.habitat: Humid subtropical rainforests, river ravines of Meghalaya and Assam, and domestic indoor pots.
85.distribution: Native to Northeast India (Meghalaya, Assam), Myanmar, and Indonesia; grown worldwide as a popular houseplant.
uses: Aerial roots trained by the indigenous Khasi and Jaintia tribes of Meghalaya to create centuries-old, living root bridges across roaring rivers
Historical source of natural rubber latex before the Amazonian rubber tree (Hevea brasiliensis) became dominant
Bold, dramatic indoor specimen plant prized for its shiny architectural foliage
careTips: Thrives in bright, indirect sunlight; can tolerate gentle morning direct sun
Water thoroughly when the top two inches of potting mix feel dry; reduce watering during winter months
Clean leaves with a soft damp cloth to keep the glossy surface free of dust and mineral deposits
85.toxicityNote: MILD-TO-MODERATE TOXICITY: The milky latex contains ficin and psoralens. Contact with skin or eyes causes irritation and dermatitis; ingestion can cause vomiting, drooling, and mouth irritation in dogs and cats.
85.funFact: The incredible Living Root Bridges of Meghalaya, some carrying foot traffic for over 500 years, are meticulously grown and woven by indigenous Khasi villagers using the living aerial roots of Ficus elastica.

86.description: A charming, long-lived woody-stemmed succulent with fleshy, teardrop-shaped jade-green leaves, revered in Feng Shui as a symbol of financial wealth, good fortune, and renewal.
identifyingFeatures: Thick, gnarled, miniature tree-like woody branching trunk giving it a natural bonsai appearance
Fleshy, plump, glossy jade-green oval or obovate opposite leaves, often developing red margins in bright sun
Clusters of tiny, delicate, star-shaped white or pale-pink flowers in late winter or early spring
Extremely durable succulent foliage capable of storing water for months of drought
86.habitat: Rocky arid scrub hills, succulent valleys, and sunny indoor balcony planters.
86.distribution: Native to KwaZulu-Natal and the Eastern Cape of South Africa; universally popular as an ornamental and feng shui plant across India.
uses: Premier Feng Shui and Vastu houseplant placed near home or office entrances to attract financial prosperity and harmony
Ideal living bonsai specimen that naturally develops an ancient, thick-trunked appearance with minimal training
Drought-resilient tabletop succulent requiring minimal maintenance
careTips: Requires at least 4-6 hours of bright direct or filtered sunlight; insufficient light causes leggy, drooping stems
Water thoroughly only when the soil has dried out completely; highly vulnerable to stem rot from overwatering
Plant in porous, gritty succulent/cactus potting mix with perlite or pumice
86.toxicityNote: TOXIC TO CATS AND DOGS: Ingestion by pets causes vomiting, depression, ataxia (unsteady gait), and slow heart rate. Keep placed on high shelves away from household pets.
86.funFact: Jade plants can live for over 70 to 100 years, often passed down through multiple family generations as living family heirlooms.

87.description: A robust, drought-conquering succulent cactus composed of flattened paddle-like green stem segments (cladodes), yellow blossoms, and sweet, juicy, spine-armed oval fruits.
identifyingFeatures: Segmented succulent shrub formed of thick, flattened, obovate green pad-like stem joints (cladodes)
Pads armed with clusters of minute, barbed hair-like bristles (glochids) and occasional sharp spines
Large, cup-shaped bright golden-yellow or orange flowers opening on the upper margins of terminal pads
Ovoid, fleshy berry fruits (tunas) ripening from green to ruby-red or purplish-crimson with sweet juicy seed-filled pulp
87.habitat: Arid deserts, dry rocky wastelands, semi-arid agricultural field boundaries, and saline scrublands.
87.distribution: Native to Mexico; naturalized extensively across arid and semi-arid regions of western and peninsular India.
uses: Nutritious sweet fruit (tunas / prickly pears) peeled and eaten fresh, rich in betalain antioxidants and Vitamin C
Tender young pads (nopales) cleaned of spines and grilled or cooked in traditional Mexican cuisine
Formidable living barbed security fence planted along rural agricultural borders to exclude cattle and wild boars
careTips: Requires full, blazing, intense direct sunshine and hot temperatures
Needs sharply draining sandy, gravelly, or rocky soil; immediately rots in waterlogged conditions
Extremely drought tolerant; requires virtually no supplemental watering once established
87.toxicityNote: Fruit flesh and pads are non-toxic and edible. MECHANICAL IRRITATION HAZARD: The tiny microscopic hair-like barbed spines (glochids) easily detach and penetrate skin or mucous membranes, causing persistent severe mechanical dermatitis, itching, and pain. Handle only with thick leather gloves or tongs.
87.funFact: Prickly pear cladodes are the traditional host plant for cochineal insects (Dactylopius coccus), the historic source of natural carmine red dye used to color royal fabrics, cosmetics, and foods.

88.description: A lush, arching graceful fern with long, feathery sword-shaped fronds bearing alternating pinnate leaflets, beloved worldwide as a classic hanging porch and indoor bathroom fern.
identifyingFeatures: Gracefully arching, pendulous pinnate fronds up to 0.5 to 1.5 meters long emerging from a central tufted crown
Alternate, closely spaced triangular-oblong leaflets (pinnae) with slightly serrated or wavy margins
Underground creeping rhizomes and thin fibrous runners producing daughter plantlets
Two neat rows of rounded spore-bearing sori protected by kidney-shaped indusia along the underside of fertile pinnae
88.habitat: Damp tropical swamps, humid shaded rock crevices, epiphytic on tree trunks, and indoor hanging pots.
88.distribution: Native to tropical forests of the Americas, West Indies, and Polynesia; universally cultivated across India.
uses: Quintessential hanging basket fern bringing lush, arching woodland greenery to verandas, living rooms, and patios
Outstanding natural humidifier and air purifier capable of absorbing indoor formaldehyde and xylene
Safe, non-toxic plant for households with dogs and cats
careTips: Requires high atmospheric humidity; mist regularly or place in naturally humid bathrooms or kitchens
Provide bright, dappled indirect light; avoid harsh direct sun which bleaches and browns frond tips
Keep potting soil consistently moist but well-drained; never allow the root ball to dry out completely
88.toxicityNote: NON-TOXIC: Completely safe and non-toxic for cats, dogs, birds, and children.
88.funFact: The popular Boston Fern originated in 1894 when a Massachusetts florist noticed a spontaneous mutation with wider, more gracefully arching and ruffled fronds among a shipment of wild sword ferns.

89.description: A stunning, shade-tolerant tropical foliage herb renowned for its lush, spear-shaped leaves beautifully patterned in silver, grey, pink, and vibrant ruby-red variegation.
identifyingFeatures: Compact, erect clumping herbaceous stems reaching 30 to 80 cm in height
Broad, elliptic-lanceolate leathery leaves with striking silver-grey feathering or vivid pink/red splashes along primary veins
Greenish-white arum-like floral spathes enclosing a pale spadix, followed occasionally by red ornamental berries
89.habitat: Tropical rainforest understories, shaded humid damp slopes, and low-light home interiors.
89.distribution: Native to the tropical rainforests of the Philippines and Sulawesi; widely grown across India as an elite indoor accent plant.
uses: Celebrated as one of the best and easiest indoor houseplants for low-light apartments and offices
Top-tier air-cleansing houseplant documented in NASA studies for filtering toxins like benzene and formaldehyde
Provides vibrant color accents indoors through contemporary pink and red cultivars (e.g., 'Siam Aurora')
careTips: Thrives in low to bright indirect light; keep entirely shielded from hot direct sun
Allow the top 2 inches of soil to dry before watering again; highly susceptible to root rot if overwatered
Keep away from cold air conditioners and drafty doorways; prefers temperatures above 16°C
89.toxicityNote: TOXIC TO PETS AND CHILDREN: Contains insoluble needle-like calcium oxalate crystals. Chewing any part causes immediate intense burning and swelling of the mouth, tongue, and throat, excessive drooling, and digestive distress.
89.funFact: In China and throughout East Asia, Aglaonema has been cultivated for centuries as an auspicious good-luck plant believed to bring good fortune, prosperity, and positive chi into the home.

90.description: A striking, upright tropical houseplant with cane-like stems and broad, dramatic emerald-green leaves intricately patterned with ivory, cream, and yellow variegation. HIGHLY TOXIC.
identifyingFeatures: Stout, fleshy, bamboo-like cane stems with prominent leaf sheath scars
Large, broad oblong-elliptic leaves marbled with creamy-white and pale yellow splotches along the center
Thick, fleshy petioles with sheathing bases clasping the central cane
Rare greenish-white spathe-and-spadix inflorescences in indoor cultivation
90.habitat: Humid tropical rainforest understory floors, shaded gullies, and domestic indoor corners.
90.distribution: Native to the tropical Americas and the West Indies; widely grown across India as an indoor foliage plant.
uses: Popular decorative indoor statement plant prized for its bold, luminous variegated leaves
Tolerates lower indoor light levels and humid living spaces
Air-filtering ornamental removing indoor airborne pollutants
careTips: Provide medium to bright indirect sunlight; direct sun burns and bleaches the variegation
Allow the top 2 inches of potting mix to dry out between waterings; avoid soggy standing water
Always wear gloves when pruning or propagating; wash hands thoroughly after handling
