90.toxicityNote: HIGHLY TOXIC: Known as 'Dumb Cane' because chewing any part causes immediate excruciating burning, intense inflammation of the tongue, lips, and vocal cords, causing temporary loss of speech ('dumbness'). Swelling can obstruct airways and cause asphyxiation. Extremely dangerous to dogs, cats, and small children.
90.funFact: The name 'Dumb Cane' refers to the horrific historical practice of punishing enslaved individuals by forcing them to chew the plant's stems, which caused their tongues to swell so violently that they were unable to speak for days.

91.description: A remarkable, drought-resilient succulent herb famous for its crenate fleshy leaves that produce tiny, rooted adventitious plantlets along their margins, and pendulous bell-like flowers.
identifyingFeatures: Fleshy, succulent cylindrical stems with thick, scalloped (crenate) opposite leaves
Unique leaf margins capable of sprouting miniature rooted baby plantlets in every scalloped notch (foliar vivipary)
Pendulous, hanging reddish-purple tubular bell-shaped flowers arranged in terminal branched cymes
Exceptional capacity to sprout new plants from a single detached leaf pinned to a wall or resting on dry soil
91.habitat: Rocky crevices, dry stone walls, sunny cottage gardens, and arid waste grounds.
91.distribution: Native to Madagascar; naturalized widely across the Indian subcontinent and tropical zones.
uses: Traditional folk remedy (Pashanbheda); in vitro and rodent assays indicate leaf extracts inhibit calcium oxalate crystal aggregation and promote diuresis. However, it cannot dissolve obstructing stones in humans, and acute urological symptoms require emergency clinical care

Traditional crushed leaf poultice applied to superficial cuts, boils, and insect bites; active flavonoids (quercetin) and bufadienolides confer validated topical anti-inflammatory and wound-healing properties
Fascinating living botany demonstration plant illustrating vegetative foliar reproduction
careTips: Requires plenty of bright sunlight to maintain compact growth and vibrant leaf margins
Extremely drought tolerant; water only when potting soil has dried out thoroughly
Simply lay a detached mature leaf flat on moist soil to propagate dozens of new plantlets
91.toxicityNote: TOXIC TO LIVESTOCK AND PETS: Contains bufadienolide cardiac glycosides (bryotoxins). Highly toxic to grazing animals, cattle, dogs, and cats, causing severe cardiac arrhythmias, tremors, vomiting, and potential heart failure. Handle with care around pets.
91.funFact: A single fallen leaf of Patharchatta can survive pinned to a bulletin board with zero soil or water for weeks while sprouting a dozen independent baby plants from its scalloped edges, earning it the title 'The Life Plant'.

92.description: A magnificent, towering annual herb with rough hairy stems, broad cordate leaves, and colossal golden composite flower heads that famously track the sun across the sky.
identifyingFeatures: Stout, erect, coarse, unbranched rough-hairy stem reaching 1.5 to 3.5 meters in height
Large, rough, ovate to cordate alternate leaves with serrate margins
Massive composite flower head (up to 30 cm across) with brilliant golden-yellow ray florets and a central disc of dark brownish-black fertile florets
Heliotropic behavior: young developing flower buds visibly follow the sun from east to west each day
92.habitat: Sunny agricultural farmlands, river plains, open meadows, and summer garden borders.
92.distribution: Native to North America; cultivated widely across southern and central India (Karnataka, Maharashtra, Andhra Pradesh).
uses: Major commercial source of healthy sunflower cooking oil, rich in polyunsaturated fats and Vitamin E
Edible roasted seeds enjoyed as wholesome snacks, rich in protein, selenium, and dietary fiber
Premier ornamental garden showstopper and crucial pollen resource for foraging honeybees
careTips: Requires full, uninterrupted, blazing sunlight (at least 6-8 hours daily)
Plant in deep, well-draining, fertile loam to accommodate a deep central taproot
Stake tall giant varieties in exposed locations to prevent lodging from heavy winds
92.toxicityNote: Non-toxic; seeds, petals, and sprouts are edible and completely safe for humans and household pets.
92.funFact: A single sunflower head is not a single flower, but an inflorescence of thousands of individual florets arranged in interlocking Fibonacci spirals, maximizing packing efficiency.

93.description: A charming, low-growing herbaceous perennial with compact rosettes of spoon-shaped leaves and cheerful solitary composite flower heads with white ray petals and sunny yellow centers.
identifyingFeatures: Basal rosette of flat, spoon-shaped (spathulate) or obovate leaves with finely scalloped margins
Slender, leafless flower scapes rising 5-15 cm above the foliage
Solitary composite flower heads with pure white (or pink-tipped) ray florets surrounding a central disc of bright golden-yellow tubular florets
Flower heads that close tightly at dusk and reopen in the morning sunshine
93.habitat: Lush lawns, temperate meadows, alpine hill station gardens (Shimla, Ooty), and ornamental borders.
93.distribution: Native to western, central, and northern Europe; cultivated across Indian hill stations and winter gardens.
uses: Classic cool-season garden edging, rockery border plant, and flowering groundcover
Tender young leaves and flower petals are edible, traditionally added to fresh spring salads
Traditional European herbal specific (Bruisewort); topical floral extracts contain polyacetylenes and saponins that assist in resolving superficial skin contusions, bruises, and muscular tenderness
careTips: Requires cool temperatures and moist, fertile, well-drained garden soil
Provide full sun in cool climates, or dappled morning light in warmer zones
Deadhead spent flowers regularly to encourage continuous blooming flushes
93.toxicityNote: Non-toxic; edible and completely safe around dogs, cats, and small children.
93.funFact: The name 'daisy' is a contraction of the Old English 'daeges eage' ('day's eye'), so called because the flower opens its petals at dawn and closes them tightly at sunset.

94.description: A tenacious, nutrient-dense perennial wild herb with deeply toothed basal leaf rosettes, bright sunny-yellow composite flower heads, and iconic spherical feathery seed puffballs.
identifyingFeatures: Basal rosette of deeply jagged, runcinate-pinnatifid leaves resembling sharp lion's teeth
Hollow, leafless cylindrical flower stalks exuding bitter milky white latex when snapped
Solitary bright golden-yellow composite flower heads composed entirely of ray florets
Spherical, ethereal seed head ('clock' or puffball) composed of hundreds of parachute-like pappus bristles attached to achenes
94.habitat: Himalayan meadows, hill station roadsides, lawn edges, pastures, and disturbed grasslands.
94.distribution: Native to Eurasia; naturalized across temperate Indian hill ranges (Kashmir, Himachal, Nilgiris) and worldwide.
uses: Tender young spring leaves eaten as a nutritious bitter salad green packed with Vitamins A, C, and K
Roasted taproots ground and brewed into a rich, caffeine-free herbal coffee substitute
Traditionally used in European herbalism as a bitter digestive tonic and gentle herbal diuretic ('pisse-en-lit') supporting fluid balance
careTips: Thrives in almost any soil and full sun; often treated as a weed due to deep taproots and windborne seeds
Deep taproots draw up mineral nutrients from subsoil layers
Harvest roots in autumn when inulin and bitter principles are most concentrated
94.toxicityNote: Non-toxic and edible. Milky latex exuded by freshly severed stems contains sesquiterpene lactones (taraxinic acid) that can cause allergic contact dermatitis in individuals sensitized to the Asteraceae family
94.funFact: The name Dandelion comes from the French 'dent-de-lion', meaning 'lion's tooth', referencing the sharply serrated, backwards-pointing teeth along the leaf margins.

95.description: A beloved aromatic evergreen semi-shrub with narrow grey-green linear foliage and elegant upright spikes of intensely fragrant lilac-purple blossoms rich in calming linalool oil.
identifyingFeatures: Compact, bushy woody-based semi-shrub reaching 30 to 60 cm in height
Opposite, narrow, linear-lanceolate greyish-green leaves with softly curled (revolute) margins covered in fragrant glandular hairs
Slender, unbranched leafless terminal stalks topped with compact spikes of small tubular two-lipped violet-purple flowers
Clean, sweet, soothing herbal-floral camphoraceous scent
95.habitat: Dry, rocky limestone slopes, Mediterranean hill pastures, and temperate Indian hill gardens (Kashmir).
95.distribution: Native to the Mediterranean region; successfully cultivated in the Kashmir Valley and Indian hill stations.
uses: Steam-distilled essential oil rich in linalool and linalyl acetate, world-renowned for aromatherapy and sleep relaxation
Dried floral buds sewn into fragrant sachets to perfume linens and deter clothing moths
Culinary herb infused into artisanal honey, gourmet lemonades, teas, and baked pastries
careTips: Requires full blazing sun (at least 6-8 hours daily) and sharply draining, gravelly, low-fertility alkaline soil
Cannot tolerate wet feet or high subtropical humidity, which induces fungal root rot
Prune lightly after summer blooming to prevent woodiness and encourage bushy growth
95.toxicityNote: Safe in culinary amounts. Ingestion of concentrated essential oils can trigger central nervous system depression and nausea in humans, and is toxic to cats and dogs who lack the glucuronidation enzymes to clear linalool and linalyl acetate.
95.funFact: The name Lavender comes from the Latin verb 'lavare' (to wash), because ancient Romans extensively perfumed their public thermal baths and laundry with fragrant lavender blossoms.

96.description: A fragrant, woody evergreen shrub with aromatic needle-like dark green leaves and delicate pale-blue blossoms, prized for culinary seasoning, hair care, and memory enhancement.
identifyingFeatures: Erect or spreading woody perennial shrub reaching 0.5 to 1.5 meters tall
Dense, needle-like, leathery linear leaves that are dark green above and silvery-white downy beneath with curled margins
Small, two-lipped pale blue to violet flowers clustered in leaf axils
Pungent, invigorating pine-wood and camphor aroma when leaves are brushed or crushed
96.habitat: Dry, sun-baked rocky Mediterranean sea-cliffs, terrace pots, and temperate herb gardens.
96.distribution: Native to the Mediterranean basin; cultivated widely in Indian kitchen herb gardens and cooler hill regions.
uses: Pungent culinary seasoning herb paired with roasted potatoes, vegetables, breads (focaccia), and oils
Traditionally used in Mediterranean folk hair care; rosemary oil rinses are reported to invigorate the scalp and promote hair vitality
Traditional symbol of remembrance; 1,8-cineole scent shown to boost cognitive recall and alertness
careTips: Needs full direct sunshine and rapid-draining gritty or sandy soil; highly susceptible to root rot if overwatered
Allow the top 2 inches of potting mix to dry between thorough waterings
Prune regularly to shape the shrub and prevent the lower stems from turning bare and woody
96.toxicityNote: Safe as a culinary seasoning. Excessive therapeutic ingestion of concentrated rosemary essential oil contains camphor and pinene which can induce severe gastrointestinal irritation, renal hyperemia, and uterine contractions, making it contraindicated during pregnancy.
96.funFact: The botanical name Rosmarinus translates poetically from Latin as 'dew of the sea' (ros = dew, marinus = sea), describing its natural habitat clinging to misty coastal Mediterranean cliffs.

97.description: A tender, aromatic annual herb with glossy, cup-shaped emerald-green leaves and an intoxicating sweet clove-anise fragrance, renowned as the soul of pesto and the source of cooling sabja seeds.
identifyingFeatures: Square, branching green stems reaching 30 to 60 cm in height
Broad, glossy, ovate leaves with smooth or slightly toothed edges, often bulging upward between veins
Whorls of small white or pale purplish flowers on terminal spikes
Tiny, oval black seeds (sabja seeds) that swell rapidly into a thick gelatinous mucilaginous coating when soaked in water
97.habitat: Warm kitchen garden plots, sunny terrace containers, and irrigated tropical herb beds.
97.distribution: Native to tropical regions of Central Africa and India; cultivated globally as a premier culinary herb.
uses: Signature herb of Mediterranean and Italian cooking: fresh Caprese salads, pasta sauces, and blended basil pesto
Black seeds (Sabja / Tukmaria) soaked in water to create cooling summer Indian faloodas, sherbets, and health drinks
Rich in natural antioxidants, eugenol, linalool, and essential aromatic terpenes
careTips: Requires warm weather and at least 6 hours of bright direct sun; highly sensitive to cold and frost
Keep potting soil moist, rich, and well-draining; avoid wetting leaves from above
Pinch off terminal flower spikes immediately as they appear to keep leaves sweet, lush, and vegetative
97.toxicityNote: Non-toxic and edible; completely safe for human culinary consumption and safe around household pets.
97.funFact: When soaked in water for just 10 minutes, sweet basil seeds (Sabja) swell to over thirty times their original volume, forming a transparent jelly bead around each seed that cools the body during hot Indian summers.

98.description: An exquisite spring-blooming bulbous perennial famous for its elegant cup-shaped blossoms in every color of the rainbow, celebrated in the sprawling tulip gardens of Kashmir.
identifyingFeatures: Tunicated subterranean bulb producing 2-6 broad, glaucous, fleshy grey-green leaves clasping the stem base
Single upright flowering scape carrying a solitary, symmetrical cup-shaped or goblet-shaped blossom
Six distinct, petal-like tepals (3 outer sepals and 3 inner petals) in solid, bicolored, or fringed hues
Six stamens with prominent dark anthers surrounding a three-lobed sessile stigma
98.habitat: Steppes, mountain valleys, temperate spring borders, and cold-winter flower beds (Indira Gandhi Memorial Tulip Garden, Srinagar).
98.distribution: Native to Central Asia and Turkey; celebrated in Kashmir, the Netherlands, and cold temperate regions globally.
uses: Premier spring ornamental cut flower and garden centerpiece worldwide
Central attraction of Kashmir's annual Tulip Festival in Srinagar, Asia's largest tulip garden
Historically the subject of 'Tulip Mania' in 17th-century Holland, the world's first recorded financial speculative bubble
careTips: Bulbs require a mandatory 12-14 week period of winter cold (below 7°C) to break dormancy and initiate flowering
Plant bulbs in autumn with pointed end up, 10-15 cm deep in loose, well-draining sandy loam
Provide full spring sunlight and moderate water; withhold watering during hot summer bulb dormancy
98.toxicityNote: TOXIC TO PETS AND HUMANS: All parts, especially the subterranean bulbs, contain allergenic lactones (tulipalin A and B) and tulipin. Ingestion causes severe vomiting, diarrhea, drooling, and depression in dogs and cats; handling bulbs can trigger 'tulip fingers' contact dermatitis.
98.funFact: During the peak of Dutch 'Tulip Mania' in February 1637, a single rare 'Semper Augustus' tulip bulb sold for the price of a luxurious grand canal house in Amsterdam before the market abruptly crashed.

99.description: A radiant spring-flowering bulb herb bearing nodding golden-yellow trumpets surrounded by six spreading perianth petals, celebrated in romantic poetry as a herald of spring.
identifyingFeatures: Tunicated subterranean ovoid bulb producing 4-6 flat, strap-like linear greyish-green leaves
Slender, flattened flowering stem bearing a solitary nodding or horizontal blossom
Six pale to golden-yellow spreading perianth segments (petals) surrounding a prominent, tubular central trumpet (corona)
Sweet delicate floral perfume and three-valved capsule containing small black seeds
99.habitat: Open woods, alpine meadows, damp riverbanks, hill station gardens, and spring borders.
99.distribution: Native to western Europe; grown in the cooler hilly climes of northern India (Kashmir, Himachal Pradesh) and temperate zones.
uses: Iconic herald of spring planted in sweeps across hill gardens, parks, and floral arrangements
Subject of William Wordsworth's immortal poem 'I Wandered Lonely as a Cloud'
Pharmaceutical extraction of the alkaloid galantamine, utilized in modern medication for Alzheimer's disease
careTips: Plant bulbs in autumn 10-15 cm deep in moist, well-draining soil with morning or full spring sun
Leave fading green foliage intact after blooming for at least 6 weeks so bulbs can photosynthesize food for next year
Naturally deer, rodent, and pest resistant due to alkaloid content
99.toxicityNote: HIGHLY TOXIC: All parts of the plant, especially the bulbs, contain toxic phenanthridine alkaloids (lycorine) and needle-like calcium oxalate crystals. Ingestion causes severe nausea, projectile vomiting, diarrhea, abdominal pain, cardiac arrhythmias, and convulsions in humans, dogs, and cats.
99.funFact: Daffodils are completely immune to garden rodents, squirrels, and deer, who instinctively avoid digging up or chewing the bulbs because of their intense toxicity.

100.description: A flamboyant, tall perennial bulb herb bearing nodding, fiery orange blossoms with recurved petals covered in dark purple-black freckles and dramatic protruding stamens. FATAL TO CATS.
identifyingFeatures: Stout, dark purplish-green leafy stem reaching 1 to 2 meters in height
Dense spirally arranged lanceolate sessile leaves with distinctive glossy black bulbils in the upper leaf axils
Nodding, unscented flowers with six strongly reflexed (curled backward) fiery orange tepals covered in raised dark brown-purple spots
Six long, spreading stamens with prominent versatile red-brown pollen anthers and a long curved pistil
100.habitat: Moist temperate valley meadows, stream banks, cool hillside gardens, and cottage borders.
100.distribution: Native to East Asia (China, Korea, Japan); grown across Indian hill stations and temperate flower gardens.
uses: Dramatic architectural summer garden perennial and premium floriculture cut flower
Starchy underground bulbs cultivated and eaten as a traditional sweet delicacy in Chinese cooking
Axillary bulbils provide effortless asexual propagation for gardeners
careTips: Requires cool, shaded roots and full to partial sunshine on top foliage ('head in sun, feet in shade')
Plant scaly bulbs in deep, humus-rich, acidic to neutral soil with impeccable drainage
Mulch soil heavily to maintain root coolness and moisture during hot summer weeks
100.toxicityNote: DEADLY HAZARD FOR CATS: True lilies (Lilium species) are EXTREMELY TOXIC AND FATAL TO CATS. Ingestion of even microscopic amounts — a bite of a leaf, licking pollen off fur, or drinking water from a vase holding cut lilies — causes rapid, irreversible acute kidney failure and death within 36-72 hours. Moderately toxic to dogs and humans (vomiting). NEVER keep true lilies in homes with cats.
100.funFact: Unlike most other lilies, the Tiger Lily produces small, glossy black pea-sized aerial bulbils in the axils of its leaves, which drop to the ground and sprout into identical clones of the parent plant.

101.description: A spectacular tuberous bushy perennial famed for its extraordinary variety of geometric, multi-layered flower heads ranging from compact pom-poms to dinner-plate-sized autumn blooms.
identifyingFeatures: Erect, hollow, branching herbaceous stems growing 1 to 2 meters tall from a cluster of starchy underground tubers
Opposite, pinnately compound or dissected leaves with ovate serrated leaflets
Spectacular composite flower heads with ray florets arranged in intricate concentric spirals in every hue except true blue
Available in forms including single, anemone, cactus, waterlily, pom-pom, and giant dinnerplate classes
101.habitat: Highland hill stations, winter gardens of the northern plains, and municipal flower show borders.
101.distribution: Native to the mountainous regions of Mexico and Central America; premier winter flower across India.
uses: Undisputed star of winter flower exhibitions and competitive horticultural shows across India
Spectacular cut flower and festive autumn/winter landscape centerpiece
Starchy tubers historically consumed as a food source by the ancient Aztecs
careTips: Requires full direct sunshine and rich, well-draining soil heavily amended with compost or well-rotted manure
Stake tall, heavy-flowering varieties early to support massive flower heads
Disbud side flower buds if aiming for giant 'dinnerplate' exhibition-sized blooms
101.toxicityNote: MILD TOXICITY: Contains phototoxic polyacetylene compounds that can cause mild skin irritation and dermatitis, as well as mild digestive upset and vomiting in dogs and cats if ingested.
101.funFact: The national flower of Mexico, Dahlias are octoploids — meaning they possess eight sets of homologous chromosomes, which accounts for their astounding diversity of flower shapes, sizes, and colors.

102.description: A rugged, sun-loving annual herb celebrated for its stiff, rough stems, sandpaper leaves, and intensely vibrant daisy-to-dahlia-like flower heads that bloom non-stop through scorching heat.
identifyingFeatures: Erect, stiff, hairy branching stems reaching 30 to 90 cm in height
Opposite, sessile, ovate-to-lanceolate rough-textured sandpaper leaves clasping the stem
Solitary composite flower heads with densely layered ray florets in vivid neon shades of magenta, scarlet, orange, yellow, and lime-green
Ring of tiny, star-shaped golden-yellow disc florets opening sequentially around the central cone
102.habitat: Hot summer flower beds, sunny borders, container gardens, and butterfly corridors.
102.distribution: Native to Mexico; cultivated ubiquitously across India as an unbeatable hot-weather garden flower.
uses: Reliable hot-weather garden bloomer that keeps flowering even in 40°C+ summer heat
Top-tier nectar magnet for monarch butterflies, swallowtails, and beneficial pollinators
Long-lasting cut flower with stiff, durable stems for colorful floral vases
careTips: Plant in full blazing sun with good air circulation to avoid powdery mildew on leaves
Water at the base of the plant early in the day; avoid wetting foliage
Deadhead faded blooms continuously to trigger rapid flushes of new buds
102.toxicityNote: NON-TOXIC: Completely safe and non-toxic for dogs, cats, horses, and children.
102.funFact: In 2016, a bright orange Zinnia became the very first flower to bloom in space, grown aboard the International Space Station's Veggie facility by astronaut Scott Kelly.

103.description: A graceful, airy annual flower with delicate feathery thread-like foliage and charming saucer-shaped blossoms in pastel pink, rose, white, and magenta swaying gently on slender wiry stems.
identifyingFeatures: Slender, multi-branching wiry stems reaching 0.6 to 1.5 meters tall
Finely dissected, feathery, bipinnate thread-like foliage giving an ethereal cloud-like texture
Saucer-shaped composite flower heads with 8 broad, notched ray florets surrounding a bright golden central disc
Slender, spindle-shaped black achene seeds tipped with tiny barbed awns
103.habitat: Sunny meadows, cottage garden borders, road verges, and empty sunny plots.
103.distribution: Native to Mexico and the southwestern US; widely naturalized and grown in winter and monsoon gardens across India.
uses: Effortless cottage-garden wildflower providing soft, billowing color sweeps
Attracts clouds of native pollinating bees, hoverflies, and butterflies to the vegetable garden
Charming, delicate cut flower for lightweight summer vases
careTips: Thrives in full sun and poor-to-average well-draining garden soil; overly rich soil produces excessive foliage at the expense of flowers
Extremely drought tolerant once established
Pinch back stem tips when young to encourage bushy branching and more flower stalks
103.toxicityNote: NON-TOXIC: Completely safe and non-toxic to dogs, cats, and humans.
103.funFact: Spanish priests in Mexico named this flower 'Cosmos' (from the Greek word for order, harmony, and universe) because of the remarkably orderly and even arrangement of its petals.

104.description: A cherished aromatic winter-flowering herbaceous perennial bearing fragrant lobed leaves and dense, showy composite flower heads in a breathtaking spectrum of autumn-winter colors.
identifyingFeatures: Bushy, branching aromatic stems reaching 30 to 90 cm in height
Alternate, deeply lobed, aromatic dark green leaves emitting a pungent herbal scent when touched
Composite flower heads ranging from single daisy forms to dense button pom-poms and spider varieties in yellow, white, bronze, pink, and red
Photoperiodic flowering triggered by shortening autumn and winter day-lengths
104.habitat: Winter exhibition gardens, suburban terrace pots, and commercial flower fields.
104.distribution: Native to East and South Asia (India, China, Japan); iconic winter flower across the northern and eastern Indian plains.
uses: Celebrated winter exhibition and garland flower (Sevanti / Chandromallika) in festive Indian winter markets

Traditional herbal tea in East Asian pharmacopoeias; dried flower infusions rich in luteolin and apigenin exhibit validated cooling, anti-inflammatory, and hepatoprotective properties in preclinical models
Long-lasting cut flower used in wedding decorations and decorative vases
careTips: Requires full direct winter sun and rich, well-draining soil with plenty of organic matter
Pinch growing tips through late summer to create a dense, spherical bush with dozens of flowering branches
Water at root base; avoid splashing water on leaves to prevent fungal rust and powdery mildew
104.toxicityNote: TOXIC TO DOGS AND CATS: Foliage contains natural pyrethrins, sesquiterpene lactones, and irritating oils. Ingestion causes vomiting, diarrhea, drooling, incoordination, and potential skin dermatitis.
104.funFact: Chrysanthemums naturally synthesize pyrethrins, organic compounds that attack insect nervous systems, making them nature's own built-in bug repellent.

105.description: A popular commercial floriculture perennial forming basal rosettes of lobed leaves and long leafless stems topped with striking, symmetrical daisy-like blooms in dazzling rainbow colors.
identifyingFeatures: Basal rosette of deeply lobed, coarse, dandelion-like leaves with woolly undersides
Tall, leafless, hollow solitary flower stalks (scapes) rising 30 to 45 cm above the foliage
Large composite flower heads with radiating, slender ray florets in brilliant red, orange, yellow, pink, and cream
Two or three concentric rings of ray petals surrounding a tight circular central disc
105.habitat: Subtropical rocky grassland slopes, polyhouse commercial farms, and potted terrace displays.
105.distribution: Native to southeastern Africa (Mpumalanga, South Africa); massively grown in commercial polyhouses across Maharashtra and Karnataka.
uses: Top-five cut flower in global floriculture, essential for wedding bouquets and stage floral arrangements
Effective indoor air-purifying plant shown in NASA studies to remove benzene, formaldehyde, and trichloroethylene
Pet-safe flowering potted plant for living rooms and verandas
careTips: Requires bright morning sun or gentle filtered light; shield from scorching summer afternoon heat
Plant with the central crown positioned slightly above soil level to prevent fatal crown rot
Water around the root zone, keeping moisture away from the crown and flower stalks
105.toxicityNote: NON-TOXIC: Completely safe and non-toxic to dogs, cats, horses, and small children.
105.funFact: Gerbera is the fifth most popular cut flower in the entire world, trailing only rose, carnation, chrysanthemum, and tulip in global trade volume.

106.description: The State Flower of Assam and Arunachal Pradesh, a magnificent monopodial epiphyte with thick leathery leaves and long pendulous, cylindrical flower clusters resembling a fluffy fox tail.
identifyingFeatures: Monopodial epiphytic growth habit with stout, climbing stems and thick, spongy silvery-white velamen-covered aerial roots
Curved, channelled, leathery strap-like leaves with uneven, praemorse (bitten-off) tips
Spectacular pendulous cylindrical racemes (up to 30-40 cm long) densely packed with over 100 miniature spotted flowers
Flowers are white to pale pink, heavily spotted and flushed with vibrant magenta-purple, emitting a sweet spicy fragrance
106.habitat: Canopy of tropical rainforest trees, mango orchards, and moist deciduous riverbanks in Northeast India and Western Ghats.
106.distribution: Native to the Indian subcontinent (Assam, Western Ghats) and Southeast Asia.
uses: Inseparable symbol of Assamese cultural identity; women wear fresh blooms in their hair during the Rongali Bihu spring dance
State Flower of Assam and Arunachal Pradesh, symbolizing love, fertility, and renewal
Collector's premier fragrant epiphytic orchid grown on driftwood or hanging wooden slat baskets
careTips: Mount on tree bark, cork slabs, or open slatted teak baskets with zero heavy potting soil
Requires high atmospheric humidity (70-80%), excellent air circulation, and bright dappled sunlight
Water or mist daily during the hot monsoon growing season; reduce watering slightly in dry winter
106.toxicityNote: Non-toxic; safe and non-hazardous to humans and domestic pets. Traditional cultural hair adornment.
106.funFact: In Assam, the flowering of Kopou Phool marks the arrival of the spring Bihu festival; according to folklore, a Bihu dancer's hair arrangement is incomplete without this sacred fox-tail blossom.

107.description: A free-floating freshwater aquatic perennial with swollen bulbous spongy petioles, glossy round leaves, and spikes of stunning pale-violet flowers bearing a peacock-eye yellow spot. Highly invasive.
identifyingFeatures: Free-floating aquatic rosette with swollen, bulbous, air-filled spongy petioles acting as natural buoyancy floats
Glossy, thick, rounded or broadly ovate dark green leaf blades
Massive, fibrous, feather-like dark purple-to-black submerged roots trailing in water
Spikes of 8-15 exquisite pale lavender-blue or violet flowers, with the top petal displaying a radiant blue halo around a bright golden-yellow spot
107.habitat: Freshwater ponds, slow-moving rivers, temple tanks, irrigation canals, and marshy lakes.
107.distribution: Native to the Amazon basin; infamously invasive weed across India, dubbed the 'Terror of Bengal'.
uses: High biomass harvested to produce biodegradable handicrafts, eco-paper, woven baskets, and green compost
Exceptional capacity for phytoremediation, absorbing heavy metals, nitrogen, and phosphorus from contaminated wastewater
Biogas production and organic agricultural mulch when properly dried and fermented
careTips: Generally prohibited from planting in natural water bodies due to severe ecological choking hazards
Floats freely on surface of water gardens in full sun
Must be contained in closed artificial tubs or ponds; never allow escape into public waterways
107.toxicityNote: Foliage contains calcium oxalate crystals causing throat burning if chewed. Wild plants bioaccumulate toxic heavy metals (lead, cadmium, arsenic) and water pathogens from polluted waters, making wild plants dangerous to ingest.
107.funFact: Dubbed the 'Terror of Bengal' in the early 20th century, its runaway growth clogged waterways, choked fish populations of oxygen, and halted river navigation throughout the Ganges-Brahmaputra delta.

108.description: A fascinating creeping herb armed with prickly stems and feathery bipinnate leaves that fold closed and droop dramatically within seconds of being touched, shaken, or heated.
identifyingFeatures: Sprawling or creeping prickly reddish-purple stems reaching 30-50 cm
Bipinnate compound leaves consisting of 1-2 pairs of pinnae, each carrying 10-26 pairs of tiny sensitive leaflets
Rapid thigmonastic (seismonastic) response: leaflets fold inward and whole petiole collapses downward upon mechanical stimulation within 1-2 seconds
Fluffy, spherical pink-to-purple powderpuff flower heads looking like miniature pompoms, followed by bristly jointed seed pods
108.habitat: Disturbed roadsides, sunny pastures, lawn edges, and tropical waste grounds.
108.distribution: Native to tropical America; widely naturalized throughout India and tropical Asia.
uses: Famous botanical curiosity demonstrating rapid plant neurobiology and turgor-driven movement (pulvini cells)
Traditional Ayurvedic specific (Lajjalu); tannin-rich root and aerial decoctions possess verified in vitro coagulation-promoting and astringent wound-healing properties
Groundcover nitrogen-fixing legume in degraded tropical soils
careTips: Requires warm temperatures (above 18°C) and full to partial sunshine
Keep soil consistently moist using well-draining loamy potting soil
Avoid triggering leaf folding excessively, as moving leaves consumes considerable biochemical energy
108.toxicityNote: TOXIC IN QUANTITY TO GRAZING LIVESTOCK: Foliage and seeds contain the non-protein amino acid mimosine, which inhibits hair follicle cell division and thyroid peroxidase. Overgrazing causes hair loss (alopecia), goiter, and emaciation in cattle and horses. Non-toxic to touch
108.funFact: The rapid folding of Mimosa pudica is caused by rapid potassium and water efflux from microscopic swollen hinge cells called pulvini at the base of every leaflet and petiole.

109.description: An aggressive, noxious invasive annual weed with carrot-like dissected leaves, angular grooved stems, and small creamy-white flower heads. SEVERE HUMAN ALLERGEN AND LIVESTOCK TOXIN.
identifyingFeatures: Erect, vigorously branching annual herb up to 1 to 2 meters tall with deeply grooved, longitudinally striated hairy stems
Deeply dissected, pale green, alternate leaves resembling carrot foliage (hence 'Carrot Grass')
Hundreds of miniature, star-shaped creamy-white flower heads (capitula) clustered in loose terminal panicles
Prolific seed producer: a single mature plant can produce up to 25,000 viable seeds
109.habitat: Wastelands, road verges, railway embankments, vacant urban lots, and agricultural fields.
109.distribution: Native to the American tropics; accidentally introduced into India in the 1950s (via PL-480 wheat imports), now a national agricultural scourge.
uses: NO BENEFICIAL USES: Recognized as one of the most hazardous alien invasive plant species in India
Subject of nationwide biological and chemical eradication campaigns using Mexican beetles (Zygogramma bicolorata)
Strictly managed and uprooted by agricultural departments to safeguard livestock and food crops
careTips: DO NOT CULTIVATE. Strict eradication weed
Must be pulled up before flowering while wearing full protective rubber gloves, masks, and long sleeves
Burn or compost safely under plastic sheeting to kill seed viability
109.toxicityNote: HIGHLY TOXIC HAZARD: Contains potent sesquiterpene lactones (chiefly parthenin). Contact triggers severe allergic contact dermatitis ('parthenium dermatitis'), eczema, facial swelling, blisters, and skin cracking in humans. Airborne pollen causes severe asthma, allergic rhinitis, and hay fever. Highly toxic to cattle, goats, and horses, causing mouth ulcers, liver damage, alopecia, and bitter, unpalatable milk.
109.funFact: Parthenium entered India in 1955 contaminated in food-aid wheat shipments from the United States under the PL-480 program, rapidly earning the moniker 'Congress Grass'.

110.description: A low-growing creeping perennial legume with creeping stolons, classic trifoliate leaves with white crescent chevrons, and rounded spherical heads of fragrant white-to-pinkish flowers.
identifyingFeatures: Creeping prostrate stems (stolons) rooting freely at the nodes to form a dense green carpet
Trifoliate leaves composed of 3 rounded obovate leaflets, usually marked with a distinct white or pale 'V'-shaped crescent watermark
Globe-shaped spherical flower heads consisting of 20-50 small pea-like white flowers, often flushed with pale pink
Sweet honey fragrance attracting vast numbers of honeybees
110.habitat: Lawns, temperate pastures, Himalayan hill station meadows, and orchard groundcover.
110.distribution: Native to Europe and central Asia; naturalized in the temperate hill ranges of northern India and worldwide.
uses: World-class nitrogen-fixing forage legume that enriches soil fertility through symbiotic rhizobia root nodules
Premier honey plant; white clover nectar produces the world's most popular light, delicate clover honey
Eco-friendly, drought-tolerant lawn alternative requiring less mowing and no synthetic nitrogen fertilizer
careTips: Prefers cool to temperate weather and moist, well-draining garden soil; struggles in scorching tropical heat
Tolerates moderate foot traffic and close mowing
Inoculate seed with Rhizobium leguminosarum before planting to maximize nitrogen fixation
110.toxicityNote: Non-toxic in small amounts. Contains cyanogenic glucosides (linamarin and lotaustralin) released upon tissue crushing, and can induce life-threatening frothy bloat in cattle when grazed as lush, wet pasture without dry roughage
110.funFact: The odds of finding a naturally occurring four-leaf clover (a genetic mutation of Trifolium repens) are estimated to be approximately 1 in 10,000, making it a universal symbol of extraordinary good luck.

111.description: A legendary, long-lived temperate hardwood canopy tree famed for its massive gnarled trunk, deeply sinuous lobed leaves, and smooth ovoid acorns held in rough scaly cups.
identifyingFeatures: Massive, rugged spreading crown with deeply fissured, greyish-brown furrowed bark
Alternate, obovate leaves with 4-7 pairs of rounded, sinuous lobes and very short petioles with distinct ear-like auricles at base
Pendulous male catkins appearing alongside fresh spring leaves
Ovoid nuts (acorns) borne on long slender stalks (peduncles), held in shallow rough scaly woody cups (cupules)
111.habitat: Temperate deciduous forests, deep fertile river valleys, and hill station botanical gardens.
111.distribution: Native to Europe, North Africa, and western Asia; cultivated in Indian Himalayan hill stations and worldwide.
uses: Premier high-density timber for historic sailing ship keels, structural architecture, and wine/whiskey aging barrels
Keystone ecological master tree supporting over 2,300 species of birds, mammals, insects, fungi, and lichens

Established in the European Pharmacopoeia; dried young bark containing up to 20% condensed tannins is approved as an astringent herbal medicine for minor inflammatory skin conditions and oral mucosal gargles.
careTips: Requires vast acreage in cool temperate climates; not suited for hot tropical lowlands
Prefers deep, rich, moisture-retentive loamy soils with unobstructed drainage
Grows slowly for centuries; requires virtually no pruning once main architectural limbs are established
111.toxicityNote: TOXIC TO HORSES, DOGS, AND CATTLE: Acorns, young leaves, and buds contain high concentrations of gallotannins and tannic acid. Ingestion by livestock or pets can cause severe gastrointestinal ulceration, bloody diarrhea, abdominal pain, and acute renal (kidney) failure. Humans must leach tannins out with water before cooking acorns.
111.funFact: An English oak tree can live for over 1,000 years: an old English proverb notes, 'Three hundred years growing, three hundred years living, and three hundred years dying.'

sources.name: EMA European Medicines Agency Herbal Monograph

112.description: A vigorous woody climbing liana famous for fragrant pendulous tubular flower clusters that open white at dusk, turn pink the next morning, and deepen into rich crimson red by afternoon to attract different pollinators.
identifyingFeatures: Clusters of pendulous star-shaped tubular flowers transitioning through white, pink, and dark red colors
Opposite, oblong to elliptic leaves with acuminated tips and distinct sunken veins
Woody climbing vine utilizing persistent spine-like petiole bases to hook onto supports
Five-winged, sharply angled woody fruit capsules ripening to dark brown
112.habitat: Secondary tropical forests, riverbanks, gardens, trellises, pergolas, and boundary fences.
112.distribution: Native to tropical Asia (India, Myanmar, Malaysia, Philippines); widely cultivated across tropical and subtropical zones globally.
uses: Highly prized ornamental pergola and fence climber valued for night fragrance and color-changing blossoms
Traditional medicine uses seeds as an anthelmintic for roundworms and pinworms (dosage caution required)
Nectar source for long-tongued hawk moths (at night) and butterflies and sunbirds (during daytime)
careTips: Provide a sturdy arbor, pergola, or trellis capable of supporting a heavy woody vine
Plant in full sun for abundant floral cascades; tolerates partial shade with fewer blooms
Water deeply during warm summer growth; prune hard in late winter before spring growth begins
112.toxicityNote: Seeds contain quisqualic acid; consuming ripe seeds in excess causes nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, and diarrhea. Leaves and flowers are considered non-toxic.
112.funFact: The flowers change color and orientation over 3 days: white and horizontal at night to attract hawk moths, then vertical and crimson by day to invite butterflies and sunbirds.

113.description: A magnificent deciduous climbing herb with tendril-tipped leaves and reflexed, wavy-margined fiery red-and-yellow flowers resembling leaping tongues of flame. It is the official state flower of Tamil Nadu.
identifyingFeatures: Showy solitary nodding flowers with 6 reflexed, wavy-margined petals starting bright yellow and maturing to brilliant crimson
Bright green lanceolate leaves ending in coiled tendril tips used for climbing
Stamens spreading widely outward horizontally with prominent versatile yellow anthers
V-shaped underground fleshy tubers containing potent alkaloids
113.habitat: Thickets, forest edges, deciduous scrub, hedges, and coastal sandy plains across peninsular India.
113.distribution: Native to tropical and southern Africa and tropical Asia, widely distributed across India, Sri Lanka, and Southeast Asia.
uses: State flower of Tamil Nadu (known as Kanthal) and national flower of Zimbabwe
Commercial industrial source of colchicine and thiocolchicoside used pharmaceutically for gout and arthritis
Important botanical in Ayurvedic medicine (Langali / Kalihari) utilized after rigorous traditional purification
careTips: Plant fleshy V-shaped tubers horizontally 8–10 cm deep in well-draining sandy loam
Provide light trellis or bamboo sticks for tendril-bearing leaf tips to grasp
Allow tubers to rest completely dry during winter dormancy; withhold water until spring shoots emerge
113.toxicityNote: HIGHLY TOXIC: All parts—especially tubers and seeds—contain lethal concentrations of colchicine. Ingestion causes severe gastrointestinal collapse, respiratory failure, organ failure, and death.
113.funFact: Gloriosa climbs not with stems or aerial roots, but with the modified tips of its leaves, which coil into sensitive grasp tendrils upon touching supports.

114.description: A vigorous tendril-climbing evergreen vine famed for fascinating cosmic-looking flowers with a wavy fringe corona, followed by aromatic, nutrient-dense purple or yellow edible fruits filled with gelatinous pulp.
identifyingFeatures: Complex intricate flowers with 5 white petals, 5 sepals, and an intense purple-and-white radiating filament corona
Deeply 3-lobed glossy alternate leaves with finely serrated margins and two glands on the petiole
Simple, unbranched axillary coiled tendrils climbing vigorously over trees and fences
Round to oval fruits with a tough outer rind ripening to deep purple or yellow, packed with pulpy seeds
114.habitat: Subtropical forest fringes, orchards, home garden arbors, and terraced slopes.
114.distribution: Native to southern Brazil, Paraguay, and northern Argentina; widely cultivated in the Western Ghats, NE India, and tropics worldwide.
uses: Major commercial fruit crop harvested for juice, desserts, mocktails, and fresh consumption
Spectacular ornamental vine for archways, privacy screens, and pollinator gardens
Rich in dietary fiber, vitamins A and C, iron, and antioxidant polyphenols
careTips: Requires full sun (at least 6 hours daily) and rich, well-draining fertile soil
Needs strong wire trellising or chain-link fencing to support heavy foliage and fruit clusters
Water consistently during flowering and fruit development; protect roots with organic mulch
114.toxicityNote: Ripe fruit pulp is delicious and completely safe. Unripe green fruits, stems, and leaves contain cyanogenic glycosides and should never be consumed raw.
114.funFact: Spanish Christian missionaries named it 'passion flower' because floral structures symbolically resembled the Passion of Christ: 3 stigmas for 3 nails, 5 anthers for 5 wounds, and the corona for the crown of thorns.

115.description: An extremely fast-growing perennial twinning creeper with distinctive palmately 5-lobed leaves and delicate lavender-to-magenta trumpet flowers, commonly seen draping railway fences and roadside hedges across India.
identifyingFeatures: Distinctive palmately divided leaves with 5 to 7 radiating lanceolate leaflets
Funnelform trumpet flowers (5–7 cm across) in shades of lavender, pale purple, or pink with a dark purple throat
Slender, glabrous twinning stems that climb swiftly over fences and smother adjacent shrubs
Smooth globular 4-valved capsule enclosing small hairy seeds
115.habitat: Railway tracks, disturbed wasteland, roadside hedges, coastal dunes, and fence lines.
115.distribution: Native to tropical Africa and Asia; naturalized pantropically across warm temperate and tropical regions.
uses: Quick-cover evergreen screen for chain-link fences, railway corridors, and boundary walls
Attracts honeybees, solitary bees, and butterflies with abundant morning nectar
Erosion control on roadside embankments and disturbed slopes
careTips: Grows vigorously in almost any soil type in full sun with minimal attention
Requires strict pruning and containment to prevent it from outcompeting weaker ornamental garden species
Drought-hardy once established; thrives in warm tropical climates without extra fertilizer
115.toxicityNote: NON-TOXIC to humans in casual contact. Ingestion of seeds in large quantities may cause mild stomach upset due to indole alkaloids typical of morning glory seeds.
115.funFact: Called 'Railway creeper' across India because colonial engineers planted it alongside railway stations and track fences to suppress dust and provide year-round green floral cover.

116.description: A graceful annual twining vine with airy, thread-like pinnatisect ferny foliage and vivid scarlet star-shaped tubular flowers beloved by hummingbirds, sunbirds, and butterflies.
identifyingFeatures: Finely dissected feather-like leaves with numerous linear, thread-like segments
Brilliant scarlet-red (rarely white or pink) 5-pointed star flowers with a long slender floral tube
Delicate twinning light-green stems winding clockwise up vertical supports
Small ovate 4-celled fruit capsules containing dark brown to black seeds
116.habitat: Cottage gardens, porch trellises, sunny balconies, hedge borders, and disturbed fields.
116.distribution: Native to tropical South and Central America; naturalized and beloved in Indian gardens for centuries.
uses: Premier ornamental vine for light trellises, hanging baskets, balcony railings, and bamboo obelisks
Exceptional pollinator plant that magnetically attracts sunbirds, hawk moths, and swallowtail butterflies
Traditional cooling folk poultices made from crushed fresh foliage for boils
careTips: Sow seeds in spring in full sun; nick seed coat or soak in warm water overnight for rapid germination
Requires light support such as twine, mesh, or thin bamboo canes to ascend
Provide moderate regular watering; avoid high-nitrogen fertilizers that encourage foliage at the expense of blooms
116.toxicityNote: Like many morning glories, the seeds contain small traces of lysergic alkaloids and can cause mild nausea if ingested in quantity. Foliage is harmless.
116.funFact: Known as 'Taralata' (Star Vine) in Bengali due to its precise five-pointed star shape that appears to twinkle against feathery emerald foliage.

117.description: A classic evergreen woody climbing vine that clings to brick, stone, and trees using adhesive aerial rootlets, featuring leathery 3-to-5 lobed dark green leaves with pale veins.
identifyingFeatures: Juvenile climbing leaves with 3 to 5 triangular lobes, glossy dark-green upper surface, and whitish veins
Adult flowering stems with unlobed rhombic leaves, small yellowish-green umbel flowers, and black berries
Dense clusters of adventitious aerial clinging rootlets emerging along the stems
Evergreen perennial habit capable of forming dense groundcovers or ascending tall brick facades
117.habitat: Temperate and subtropical woodlands, masonry walls, shaded garden borders, and indoor terrariums.
117.distribution: Native to Europe, western Asia, and northern Africa; cultivated worldwide as an ornamental vine and indoor houseplant.
uses: Popular trailing indoor houseplant famous for high air-filtration efficiency (benzene, formaldehyde)
Groundcover for deep shade under trees where grass refuses to grow
Masonry cover providing thermal insulation to exterior stone buildings
careTips: Thrives in bright indirect light to medium shade indoors; avoid scorching direct afternoon sun
Allow top inch of potting mix to dry between waterings; avoid soggy waterlogged soil
Wipe leaves occasionally with a damp cloth to remove dust and discourage spider mites
117.toxicityNote: MILDLY TOXIC: Leaves and berries contain triterpenoid saponins (hederagenin). Ingestion can cause vomiting, diarrhea, and salivation in pets; sap may cause contact dermatitis.
117.funFact: English ivy shows dramatic heterophylly: while juvenile vines climbing walls have 3–5 lobed leaves, mature branches that reach sunlight produce unlobed oval leaves and flowers.

118.description: A robust, sprawling tropical climbing shrub with glossy whorled leaves and large, luminous golden-yellow trumpet-shaped blossoms with a fruity fragrance.
identifyingFeatures: Large brilliant golden-yellow bell-shaped flowers (8–12 cm wide) with orange-yellow throat stripes
Glossy, leathery oblong-lanceolate leaves arranged in whorls of 4 along stout green stems
Exudes a sticky white milky latex from all broken tissues
Prickly, spiny globular seed capsules (burr-like) containing winged flat seeds
118.habitat: Tropical gardens, coastal resorts, roadside hedges, fences, and warm verandas.
118.distribution: Native to Brazil and tropical America; naturalized throughout the tropics including coastal India and Southeast Asia.
uses: Spectacular flowering vine for fences, pergolas, porticos, and driveway entrance gates
Provides uninterrupted flowering throughout tropical summer and monsoon seasons
Attracts carpenter bees, hawkmoths, and butterflies
careTips: Requires full tropical sun (6+ hours daily) for profuse continuous blooming
Water regularly during active growth; allow topsoil to dry slightly between watering cycles
Prune vigorously in early spring to encourage bushy branching and fresh flowering wood
118.toxicityNote: TOXIC: All parts of the plant and its milky sap contain iridoid lactones (allamandin). Ingestion causes violent vomiting, stomach cramps, and diarrhea. Sap causes skin irritation.
118.funFact: The specific epithet 'cathartica' is derived from the Greek 'katharsis' (purging), referencing historical medicinal use as a drastic emetic and purgative.

119.description: An enchanting evergreen twinning climber producing lantern-like inflated snowy white calyces from which emerge bright crimson corolla lobes with long protruding stamens, giving the impression of drops of blood.
identifyingFeatures: Hanging floral cymes consisting of inflated pure-white pouch calyces and contrasting blood-red petals
Slender floral stamens and styles protruding 2–3 cm far beyond the crimson petals
Opposite, dark emerald ovate leaves with prominent depressed veins and smooth margins
Slender, woody twining stems that climb gracefully without thorns or tendrils
119.habitat: Tropical shaded borders, conservatory arbors, balcony grills, and sheltered humid verandas.
119.distribution: Native to tropical West Africa (Cameroon to Senegal); cultivated worldwide in tropical and warm subtropical gardens.
uses: High-contrast ornamental climber for shaded trellises, balcony grills, and hanging baskets
Outstanding container patio specimen trained on wire topiary hoops
Nectar source for butterflies and hoverflies
careTips: Prefers bright dappled light or morning sun; protect from harsh afternoon sun which bleaches white calyces
Maintain consistently moist, organically rich, well-draining soil
Pinch back stem tips after blooming to encourage bushier growth and multi-stem flower heads
119.toxicityNote: NON-TOXIC to cats, dogs, and humans. Safe for family households and pet-friendly indoor gardens.
119.funFact: Named by botanist William Balfour Baikie in honor of the late wife of Rev. William Cooper Thomson, a Scottish missionary and physician in Old Calabar, Nigeria.

120.description: A spectacular vigorous evergreen woody tendril-climber that blankets roofs, fences, and pergolas in a dazzling sea of tubular fiery-orange flowers throughout winter and early spring.
identifyingFeatures: Dense hanging clusters of bright orange, slender tubular blossoms with reflexed petal lobes
Compound leaves with 2 to 3 ovate leaflets and a terminal 3-parted branched climbing tendril
Vigorous branching woody stems climbing up to 15 meters over walls and trees
Exserted yellow stamens extending beyond the narrow curved orange floral tube
120.habitat: Subtropical garden walls, roof pergolas, driveway arches, and sunny hillside fences.
120.distribution: Native to southern Brazil, Bolivia, Paraguay, and Argentina; widely grown across India (especially Bangalore and Pune) and global tropics.
uses: Premier winter-flowering ornamental vine covering boundary walls, carports, and overhead trellises
Provides vital winter nectar for honeybees, sunbirds, and hummingbirds when few other plants bloom
Fast erosion cover for exposed tropical banks
careTips: Plant in full blazing sun to ensure maximum flower development; shaded plants produce only leaves
Water regularly during establishment, but tolerates dry spells once rooted
Prune heavily immediately after winter flowering ends to keep growth under control
120.toxicityNote: NON-TOXIC to humans and domestic animals under normal circumstances.
120.funFact: The genus name 'Pyrostegia' comes from Greek 'pyr' (fire) and 'stege' (covering/roof), literally describing its habit of covering entire building roofs in fiery orange blossoms.

121.description: A vigorous perennial woody twining climber native to northeastern India, famous for pendulous racemes of large, pale lavender-blue or sky-blue trumpet flowers with pale yellow throats.
identifyingFeatures: Large trumpet-shaped sky-blue to lavender flowers (up to 8 cm across) with creamy-yellow throats in hanging racemes
Opposite, rough-textured cordate leaves with pointed lobes and prominent tooth-like serrations
Vigorous rope-like twinning woody stems with massive underground tuberous root storage systems
Globular beak-tipped fruit capsules that fling seeds outward upon drying
121.habitat: Moist deciduous forests, river valleys, large garden pergolas, and highway trellises.
121.distribution: Native to northeastern India (Bengal, Assam), Bangladesh, and southern China; cultivated across the world's tropics.
uses: Spectacular heavy pergola and gazebo vine offering dense green shade and cascading blue flowers
Traditional poultices from leaves used in folk remedies for snake bites and stomach aches in Assam
Favorite nectar plant for carpenter bees and large swallowtail butterflies
careTips: Requires substantial arbor or metal pergola structure capable of carrying large woody weight
Thrives in fertile, organically rich, moist but well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade
Prune hard in late winter or early spring to manage massive vegetative spread
121.toxicityNote: NON-TOXIC: Safe around children and domestic pets. No reported human or animal toxicities.
121.funFact: Native to the tea-growing hill regions of Bengal and Assam, it can grow up to 20 meters tall into forest canopy trees with tuberous roots that can weigh over 50 kilograms.

122.description: A rapid-growing tendril-climbing perennial vine with arrow-shaped wavy leaves and profusely blooming branched racemes of vivid coral-pink or rose-colored floral clusters that terminate in delicate clinging tendrils.
identifyingFeatures: Arching panicles of dainty, bright coral-pink flowers with petal-like sepals
Floral branch tips ending in branching, coiled climbing tendrils
Crinkled, wavy arrow-shaped or heart-shaped (cordate) alternate leaves with prominent reticulate veins
Underground edible tuberous rootstocks that allow survival through severe dry spells
122.habitat: Disturbed urban fences, railway borders, tropical gardens, coastal slopes, and sunny walls.
122.distribution: Native to Mexico and Central America; naturalized and abundant throughout India, Southeast Asia, and Pacific islands.
uses: Popular flowering fence and arbor cover blooming year-round in frost-free tropical gardens
Major nectar and pollen source for honeybees; produces light aromatic honey
Traditional tea brewed from aerial parts in Mexican folk medicine for coughs and flu
careTips: Thrives in full sun and handles poor, rocky, or sandy soils with high heat tolerance
Water moderately; highly drought-tolerant once tuberous roots establish
Cut back severely to ground level in winter or early spring if vine becomes messy or overgrown
122.toxicityNote: NON-TOXIC: Tubers are roasted and eaten in rural Mexico. Safe for children and household animals.
122.funFact: Referred to as 'Chain of Love' across the Caribbean because each delicate flowering branch ends in a tender heart-shaped spray with climbing tendrils.

123.description: A vibrant evergreen tropical shrub renowned worldwide for thick, leathery glossy leaves showcasing an astonishing mosaic of colors including fiery scarlet, amber yellow, bright orange, bronze, and deep forest green.
identifyingFeatures: Thick, leathery, glossy leaves displaying dramatic multicolored patterns (red, yellow, orange, green, purple)
Enormous diversity in leaf shapes (broad ovate, ribbon-like, twisted spiral, or oak-leaf lobed) across cultivars
Exudes a clear-to-milky sap when stems or leaves are snapped
Inconspicuous small white star-like male and female flowers in long axillary racemes
123.habitat: Tropical shrub borders, foundation plantings, hotel lobbies, and bright indoor verandas.
123.distribution: Native to Indonesia, Malaysia, Australia, and western Pacific islands; ubiquitous as an ornamental across India.
uses: Top tropical landscape accent shrub providing year-round vibrant color without relying on flowers
Popular indoor and patio potted specimen for well-lit rooms and corporate atriums
Traditional hedge planting along boundary fences and pathways
careTips: Requires bright indirect light or several hours of direct morning sun to maintain vivid leaf coloration
Keep soil evenly moist using room-temperature water; avoid letting roots sit in standing saucers
Maintain high humidity; mist leaves regularly or place over pebble trays in air-conditioned interiors
123.toxicityNote: TOXIC: Plant sap contains phorbol esters. Ingestion can cause severe mouth irritation, vomiting, and diarrhea. Sap causes contact eczema and skin rash.
123.funFact: In Bengali it is called 'Patabahar' (Joy of Leaves) because its ever-changing multicolored foliage provides the visual impact of an eternal spring garden without flowers.

124.description: A popular indoor trailing or climbing evergreen aroid characterized by juvenile arrow-shaped leaves with silver, cream, or pink variegation, transforming into multi-lobed leaves as it matures.
identifyingFeatures: Juvenile leaves distinctly arrow-shaped (sagittate) with pale mint-green or silvery-white centers
Mature leaves dividing into 3 to 5 distinct radiating finger-like leaflets as the vine climbs
Slender creeping or climbing green stems equipped with aerial roots at each node
Typical aroid inflorescence of greenish spathes enclosing cream spadices (rare indoors)
124.habitat: Tropical rainforest understories, moss poles, hanging baskets, and indoor water propagation jars.
124.distribution: Native to tropical America (Mexico to Bolivia); grown globally as one of the most resilient indoor plants.
uses: Top air-purifying indoor houseplant effective in removing airborne formaldehyde and toluene
Ideal for hanging baskets, moss-pole climbing displays, and terrarium enclosures
Can be grown indefinitely in simple glass jars of clean water without soil
careTips: Thrives in medium to bright indirect light; tolerates low-light conditions with slower growth
Water when the top 2–3 cm of potting soil feels dry; reduce frequency during winter
Provide a coir or moss pole if you want the vine to climb and develop larger mature leaves
124.toxicityNote: TOXIC TO PETS: Contains insoluble calcium oxalate crystals. Chewing foliage causes intense mouth irritation, drooling, burning sensations of lips and tongue, and difficulty swallowing.
124.funFact: Syngonium undergoes complete leaf metamorphosis: young plants kept in pots remain compact arrowheads, but when allowed to climb a tall tree in the wild, leaves divide into 5–9 large separate leaflets.

125.description: An enduring, beginner-friendly indoor climbing or trailing evergreen vine featuring smooth, deep-green, heart-shaped leaves with long pointed tips that cascade gracefully from shelves and baskets.
identifyingFeatures: Perfectly cordate (heart-shaped) glossy leaves with extended tapering pointed tips (drip tips)
Emerging juvenile leaves often emerge with a distinctive bronze or coppery-pink translucence
Flexible, slender trailing stems bearing small aerial root nubs at leaf nodes
Translucent paper-like leaf sheaths (cataphylls) that dry and persist along stems
125.habitat: Neotropical humid rainforest canopies, mossy tree trunks, bookshelf planters, and hanging baskets.
125.distribution: Native to Central America and the Caribbean; cultured globally as one of the most widely kept houseplants.
uses: Premier trailing houseplant for office desks, high bookshelves, and macramé hanging planters
Demonstrated in NASA Clean Air Study to remove indoor air pollutants like formaldehyde
Excellent for terrariums, vivarium backgrounds, and green vertical living walls
careTips: Adaptable to low, medium, or bright indirect light; keep shielded from harsh scorching sun
Water when top half of potting soil is dry; remarkably forgiving of occasional forgotten watering
Prune leggy trailing vines just above a node to stimulate dense bushy growth at the crown
125.toxicityNote: TOXIC: Contains insoluble needle-like calcium oxalate raphides. Ingestion causes oral pain, burning of lips and tongue, vomiting, and excessive drooling in dogs and cats.
125.funFact: The name Philodendron comes from the Greek 'philo-' (love) and 'dendron' (tree), describing its natural passion for clinging lovingly to tropical rainforest tree trunks.

126.description: A magnificent large architectural evergreen aroid featuring massive, deeply incised, wavy-margined glossy leaves and a stout trunk covered in striking eye-like leaf scars and thick aerial roots.
identifyingFeatures: Enormous leathery glossy leaves (up to 1 m long) deeply pinnately lobed with wavy, undulating margins
Heavy, stout semi-woody trunk marked with distinctive oval eye-shaped drop scars from fallen leaves
Long, fleshy, rope-like aerial roots anchoring into soil from upper trunk nodes
Large brownish-purple spathe surrounding a cream-colored spadix that produces metabolic heat during bloom
126.habitat: Subtropical forest floors, swamp margins, shady villa courtyards, and large living room corners.
126.distribution: Native to tropical South America (southeastern Brazil, Bolivia, Paraguay, Argentina); popular landscape plant in warm regions.
uses: Dramatic architectural statement plant for tropical landscaping, luxury courtyards, and hotel lobbies
Effective outdoor shaded ground cover and foundation border in frost-free climates
Excellent long-lived large container specimen for bright patios and verandas
careTips: Give ample floor space to accommodate its wide, spreading sculptural canopy
Provide bright indirect light or dappled sunlight; tolerates morning sun well
Keep soil consistently moist during warm months, allowing surface to dry slightly between waterings
126.toxicityNote: TOXIC: Contains microscopic calcium oxalate crystals. Chewing cause burning sensation of tongue and throat, vomiting, and swelling of the pharynx in pets.
126.funFact: Flowers of Thaumatophyllum can generate their own heat through thermogenesis, heating up to 45°C (113°F) above ambient air to volatilize scents and attract pollinating scarab beetles.

127.description: A slow-growing woody evergreen shrub producing thick cane-like stems topped with graceful rosettes of broad, arching glossy green strap leaves, frequently variegated with a central lime-yellow stripe.
identifyingFeatures: Stout woody gray canes (stems) topped with crown clusters of arching sword-shaped leaves
Broad glossy ribbon leaves with wavy margins, commonly sporting a broad central golden-yellow band ('Massangeana')
Highly fragrant nocturnal flowers in rounded pom-pom panicles followed by orange berries (rare indoors)
Upright architectural silhouette ideal for indoor corners
127.habitat: Upland tropical rainforests of Africa, shaded understories, office buildings, and living spaces.
127.distribution: Native to tropical Africa (Sudan to Mozambique and Angola); cultivated worldwide as one of the most common houseplants.
uses: Stalwart commercial interior plant favored for corporate offices and home living areas
High ranking on NASA clean air tests for removal of indoor volatile compounds (xylene, formaldehyde)
Low-maintenance structural accent for low-light indoor corners
careTips: Thrives in medium to bright indirect light; survives surprisingly well in lower-light indoor areas
Water thoroughly only when the top 50% of potting mix is dry; sensitive to overwatering and fluoride in tap water
Use filtered or rainwater if leaf tips turn brown due to chlorine and fluoride sensitivity
127.toxicityNote: TOXIC TO CATS AND DOGS: Contains steroidal saponins. Ingestion causes vomiting (occasionally with blood), depression, anorexia, hypersalivation, and dilated pupils in cats.
127.funFact: Named 'fragrans' (fragrant) because its nocturnal blossoms release an intoxicating sweet jasmine-honey perfume that can fill an entire household.

128.description: A striking architectural evergreen shrub with densely spiraling lance-shaped leaves dramatically edged in bright golden yellow and lime green on irregularly branching woody stems.
identifyingFeatures: Dense, alternating whorls of stiff, pointed lanceolate leaves spiraling around woody stems
Rich dark-green leaf centers bordered by broad, luminous golden-yellow and cream margins ('Variegata')
Characteristic reflexed (downward curling) leaf tips giving the foliage a flowing fountain appearance
Multiple branching woody stems creating a bushy, sculptural silhouette
128.habitat: Coastal thickets and tropical forests of Indian Ocean islands; popular in tropical landscape borders and indoor atriums.
128.distribution: Native to Mozambique, Madagascar, Mauritius, and adjacent Indian Ocean islands; cultivated pantropically.
uses: High-end decorative indoor foliage plant that adds bright golden highlights to modern interior designs
Top-performing outdoor border shrub and hedge in frost-free tropical gardens
Effective natural indoor air purifier absorbing benzene, toluene, and trichloroethylene
careTips: Requires bright indirect sunlight to preserve vivid golden leaf margins; fades to dull green in deep shade
Allow top 3–4 cm of soil to dry between waterings; avoid standing water in decorative outer pots
Prune tall branches in spring to stimulate fresh multi-stem bushy growth lower down the canes
128.toxicityNote: TOXIC TO PETS: Contains steroidal saponins toxic to dogs and cats. Ingestion results in drooling, vomiting, loss of appetite, and lethargy.
128.funFact: Despite its worldwide trade name 'Song of India', this species is not actually native to India, but to Madagascar and the Mascarene Islands of the Indian Ocean.

129.description: An exotic epiphytic evergreen tropical perennial celebrated for heart-shaped, glossy patent-leather-like spathes in vivid red, coral, or pink, centered by a slender upright creamy-yellow spadix.
identifyingFeatures: Heart-shaped (cordate) waxy, glossy modified leaf bract (spathe) with a lacquered plastic-like sheen
Straight, cylindrical, tail-like central floral spike (spadix) carrying hundreds of tiny true flowers
Deep emerald-green leathery arrow-to-heart-shaped foliage held on long, stiff petioles
Epiphytic climbing habit producing fleshy aerial roots in humid environments
129.habitat: Neotropical montane cloud forests, warm humid shade-houses, and modern indoor living spaces.
129.distribution: Native to southwestern Colombia and northwestern Ecuador; hybridized and cultivated globally.
uses: Premier cut flower celebrated for unrivaled vase life of 4 to 6 weeks in floral arrangements
Elite flowering houseplant providing continuous blooms practically all year round indoors
NASA Clean Air Study plant showing high absorption rates of formaldehyde, ammonia, and xylene
careTips: Needs bright, warm, filtered indirect light; never expose to direct sun which scorches waxy spathes
Pot in coarse, highly aerated orchid-bark mix (peat, perlite, bark chunks) to prevent root suffocation
Keep humidity above 50%; mist foliage or set on humidity trays; water when top inch of bark feels dry
129.toxicityNote: TOXIC: Entire plant contains insoluble calcium oxalate needles. Ingestion causes intense burning of mouth and throat, voice loss (aphonia), blistering, and gastric pain.
129.funFact: What is commonly called the Anthurium 'flower' is actually a modified leaf called a spathe; the true flowers are microscopic bumps lining the central yellow pencil-like spadix.

130.description: An iconic architectural evergreen perennial producing stiff, banana-like gray-green leaves and spectacular blossoms resembling the crested head of an exotic tropical crane with fiery orange sepals and vivid purple-blue petals.
identifyingFeatures: Inflorescence emerging from a horizontal, boat-shaped woody spathe (beak) perched atop a tall leafless stalk
Dramatic floral crest of 3 brilliant orange sepals and 3 electric blue petals resembling an exotic bird plumage
Clumping habit of long-petioled, paddle-shaped glaucous green leaves resembling small banana leaves
Hard, round black seeds bearing a bright orange fuzzy aril (seed coat)
130.habitat: Coastal thickets, riverine bush, subtropical garden lawns, and sunny greenhouse atriums.
130.distribution: Native to eastern coast of South Africa (KwaZulu-Natal and Eastern Cape); iconic landscape plant worldwide.
uses: World-renowned luxury landscape accent plant and architectural feature for modern estates
Prestigious cut flower in international floriculture trade lasting weeks in arrangements
Official city flower of Los Angeles, California
careTips: Requires bright sun (4 to 6 hours direct sunlight daily) to produce flowers; will not bloom in dark rooms
Plant in deep, rich, well-draining soil mix; water deeply during warm season, allowing surface to dry between waterings
Feed monthly during active spring and summer growth with a balanced liquid fertilizer
130.toxicityNote: MILDLY TOXIC: Seeds and fruit contain toxic tannins and unknown alkaloids causing mild vomiting, diarrhea, and drowsiness in dogs and cats if ingested.
130.funFact: In nature, the flowers are pollinated by sunbirds that perch on the boat-shaped spathe; their body weight pushes down the blue petals, dusting pollen onto the bird's feet and chest.

131.description: A rapid-growing trailing perennial succulent herb featuring ovate leaves striped in glittering metallic silver and olive green on the upper surface, with a rich, uniform magenta-purple underside.
identifyingFeatures: Foliage upper surface marked by two broad glittering silver-white longitudinal bands flanking a green center
Underside of leaves and succulent stems uniformly colored a rich royal purple or magenta
Small 3-petaled bright pink-to-magenta flowers appearing sporadically between leaf bracts
Succulent trailing stems rooting eagerly at every joint or leaf node touching soil
131.habitat: Tropical wet forests, rocky riverbanks, indoor hanging baskets, and shady garden borders.
131.distribution: Native to southern Mexico, Central America, and Colombia; grown globally as an effortless trailing houseplant.
uses: Premier hanging basket plant providing cascading ribbons of shimmering purple and silver foliage
Groundcover for frost-free shaded tropical gardens and understory borders
One of the easiest plants to propagate in water or soil for novice gardeners
careTips: Thrives in bright indirect sunlight; higher light produces deeper purple pigmentation and brighter silver stripes
Water thoroughly when top 2–3 cm of soil is dry; avoid letting water sit on fuzzy leaf surfaces
Pinch back stem tips regularly to prevent trailing vines from becoming bare or leggy near the soil
131.toxicityNote: MILDLY TOXIC TO PETS: Sap contains microscopic calcium oxalate raphides. Contact causes skin irritation, itching, and redness (contact dermatitis) in cats and dogs.
131.funFact: Called 'Inch plant' because the stems grow so fast they seem to gain an inch every few days, and a tiny one-inch stem cutting can root and become a full plant within weeks.

132.description: An elegant evergreen tree featuring gracefully drooping slender branches laden with dense, glossy, oval pointed leaves, widely cultivated both as a stately outdoor avenue tree and an indoor potted specimen.
identifyingFeatures: Arching, pendulous (weeping) branchlets bearing glossy, leathery pointed oval leaves with an acuminated drip-tip
Smooth light gray bark on trunk and major branches
Abundant sticky white milky latex released from any damaged bark, leaf, or twig
Small round figs (syconia) borne in pairs, ripening from green to orange-red and purple-black
132.habitat: Monsoon tropical forests, riverbanks, city parks, residential avenues, and indoor atriums.
132.distribution: Native to India, southern China, Southeast Asia, Malaysia, and northern Australia; planted worldwide.
uses: One of the most famous indoor topiary trees, often grown with intricately braided trunks
Stately shade and avenue tree across Indian cities providing extensive canopy and bird forage
Noted effectiveness in NASA clean air trials for removing gaseous formaldehyde and xylene
careTips: Requires bright, stable indirect sunlight; sensitive to being moved and may drop leaves if relocated abruptly
Water when the top 3 cm of soil is dry; reduce watering frequency during cool winter months
Avoid cold drafts, air conditioning vents, and sudden environmental changes to prevent leaf shed
132.toxicityNote: MILDLY TOXIC: Milky latex sap contains ficin and furocoumarins. Can cause skin irritation and rash; ingestion causes gastrointestinal upset, vomiting, and drooling in pets.
132.funFact: The weeping fig is the official state tree of Bangkok, Thailand, where gigantic multi-trunked specimens shade temples and canals.

133.description: A delicate, scrambling evergreen perennial climber characterized by feathery, cloud-like horizontal sprays of ultra-fine needle-like modified stems (cladodes) resembling delicate lace.
identifyingFeatures: Flat horizontal triangular tiers of airy, feathery, needle-like green branchlets (cladodes)
Slender, wiry climbing green stems bearing small backward-pointing sharp spines (modified true leaves)
Tiny greenish-white bell-shaped flowers borne at the branchlet tips, followed by small round berries turning black
Fleshy, tuberous root system allowing survival during dry spells
133.habitat: Rainforest understories, shaded coastal valleys, floral greenhouse benches, and living room planters.
133.distribution: Native to southern and eastern Africa; cultivated worldwide as an ornamental houseplant and floral filler.
uses: Essential green filler in the global floral arrangement industry, adding ethereal texture to bridal bouquets
Popular indoor specimen for bookshelves, terrariums, and bathroom window sills
Trellised climber for shady tropical courtyard walls and sheltered veranda borders
careTips: Prefers bright dappled light or soft morning sun; harsh direct sunlight scorches and yellows needle cladodes
Keep soil evenly moist but never waterlogged; mist frequently to simulate humid rainforest conditions
Trim yellowing or overgrown wiry canes at the soil line to stimulate fresh emerald fronds from the crown
133.toxicityNote: TOXIC TO CATS AND DOGS: Contains sapogenins. Repeated skin contact causes allergic dermatitis; ingestion of the black berries causes gastric pain, vomiting, and diarrhea.
133.funFact: Despite its common name 'Lace Fern', this plant is not a true fern at all—it does not reproduce via spores, but is a flowering seed plant belonging to the Asparagus family.

134.description: A graceful clumping multi-stemmed feather palm with golden-yellow petioles, slender bamboo-like canes, and arching feathery fronds, celebrated as one of the world's most popular indoor and landscape palms.
identifyingFeatures: Multiple clustering slender, ringed bamboo-like green canes rising in a tight vase-shaped clump
Gracefully arching feather fronds (pinnate) with 80 to 100 narrow, lanceolate leaflets
Distinctive golden-yellow to orange-yellow coloring on petioles and crownshaft sheaths
Panicles of small yellow flowers followed by small yellow-to-purple oval fruits
134.habitat: Coastal sand dunes, tropical riverbanks, hotel atriums, garden lawns, and indoor office courtyards.
134.distribution: Native to eastern Madagascar; cultivated universally across tropical, subtropical, and indoor locations globally.
uses: Foremost indoor potted palm worldwide, celebrated for naturalizing interior architecture with lush tropical grace
Top-ranked plant in NASA clean air research for humidifying dry indoor air and absorbing airborne toxics
Excellent dense outdoor privacy screen and tropical boundary hedge in warm climates
careTips: Thrives in bright indirect light; can tolerate mild morning sun outdoors, but avoid scorching afternoon rays
Water when top 2–3 cm of potting soil dries out; ensure planter drainage holes are completely clear
Flush potting soil occasionally with distilled or rainwater to prevent brown leaf tips caused by fluoride and mineral salts
134.toxicityNote: NON-TOXIC: Completely safe and non-toxic to dogs, cats, and humans. Certified pet-friendly houseplant.
134.funFact: While endangered in its native wild riverbank habitats of Madagascar, it has become one of the most commercially propagated plants on planet Earth with millions grown annually in nurseries.
