135.description: A majestic clumping semi-evergreen perennial herb with glossy arrow-shaped leaves and pure-white trumpet-shaped funnel spathes enclosing a bright golden spadix.
identifyingFeatures: Pristine, creamy-white funnel-shaped floral spathe with a gentle flare and recurved tip
Central upright, bright yellow-orange cylindrical spadix covered in tiny true blossoms
Large, lush arrow-to-heart-shaped (sagittate) emerald-green leaves on long fleshy spongy stems
Thick underground rhizomatous tuberous root system
135.habitat: Stream margins, marshy meadows, garden water features, damp ditches, and cool conservatory beds.
135.distribution: Native to southern Africa (Lesotho, South Africa, Eswatini); naturalized on multiple continents.
uses: Iconic wedding flower and floral arrangement centerpiece symbolizing purity and timeless sophistication
Stunning marginal aquatic accent for garden ponds, water features, and damp bog gardens
Container patio display for spring and summer blooming
careTips: Enjoys full sun in cool climates, or morning sun with afternoon shade in hot tropical regions
Requires abundant moisture; thrives with soil kept consistently moist or standing in shallow pond water margins
Protect rhizomes from heavy freezing frost; mulch well in winter or store dormant tubers indoors
135.toxicityNote: TOXIC: Contains sharp insoluble calcium oxalate crystals. Ingestion produces immediate burning of lips, tongue, and throat, vomiting, difficulty swallowing, and excessive drooling in animals.
135.funFact: The calla lily is neither a true lily (Liliaceae) nor a calla; Swedish botanist Carl Linnaeus placed it in the genus Calla, but it was later moved to Zantedeschia, named in honor of Italian botanist Giovanni Zantedeschi.

136.description: An evergreen coniferous tree or large conical shrub revered in Indian gardens, characterized by dense, vertical, fan-like planar sprays of bright green scale-like foliage resembling the feathers of a peacock.
identifyingFeatures: Branchlets arranged in distinctive flat, vertical, fan-shaped planar sprays
Tiny, overlapping scale-like leaves with a gland along the back, emitting a resinous aroma when bruised
Ovoid-globular fleshy cones (1.5–2.5 cm) ripening from glaucous blue-green to woody brown with recurved horn-like scales
Neat, formal conical to columnar crown habit with reddish-brown fibrous shredding bark
136.habitat: Temple courtyards, residential front gardens, formal hedges, rocky limestone hills, and bonsai collections.
136.distribution: Native to northwestern China, Korea, and eastern Russia; widely planted across India, Central Asia, and warm temperate zones.
uses: Auspicious residential garden tree in India, traditionally associated with wisdom and placed in schoolbooks for good luck
Popular formal hedge, topiary, and living boundary screen due to its dense, neat vertical foliage
Important herb in Traditional Chinese Medicine (Baizi / Ce Bai Ye) for promoting hair health and calming nerves
careTips: Plant in full sun for tightest foliage density and richest green coloration; tolerates light shade
Thrives in well-drained, moderately fertile soil; extremely tolerant of alkaline limestone soils and urban smog
Drought-hardy once established; avoid poorly drained clay where stagnant water can cause root rot
136.toxicityNote: NON-TOXIC to humans under normal landscape exposure. Foliage contains thujone essential oils that may cause mild digestive discomfort in pets if chewed in large amounts.
136.funFact: Across northern and central India, school children traditionally tuck Morpankhi leaf sprays inside textbook pages, affectionately believing it sharpens memory and exam performance.

137.description: A profusely blooming tropical evergreen shrub characterized by unique spoon-shaped or fiddle-shaped leaves and dense bouquets of pristine snow-white flowers with bright yellow centers, retaining foliage year-round.
identifyingFeatures: Distinctive fiddle-shaped or spoon-shaped leaves with narrow bases and flared, lobed tips
Dense terminal clusters of pure white 5-petaled flowers with a small yellow eye, largely unscented
Evergreen or semi-evergreen habit, retaining foliage much longer into winter than Plumeria rubra
Smooth grayish-green succulent stems exuding milky white latex when cut
137.habitat: Tropical residential gardens, median strips, temple courtyards, and container patio displays.
137.distribution: Native to Colombia, Panama, and Venezuela; massively popular and cultivated across India, Thailand, and the tropics.
uses: One of the best landscape shrubs for continuous, non-stop white floral displays throughout the year in India
Popular ornamental shrub for residential entranceways and temple gardens
Used for floral garlands, altar offerings, and floating bowl decorations
careTips: Requires full tropical sun (at least 6 hours daily) for maximum flowering performance
Water moderately; allow the soil to dry out between waterings to prevent root and stem rot
Prune lightly to shape and encourage multiple flowering branch tips
137.toxicityNote: MILDLY TOXIC: Like all members of the Apocynaceae family, the white milky latex sap can irritate skin and eyes. Ingestion causes stomach upset in pets.
137.funFact: Known as 'Nag Champa' in India because the unusual flared shape of its leaf apex closely resembles the expanded hood of a cobra (Nag).

138.description: A beautiful evergreen flowering shrub native to India, renowned for glossy dark-green leaves and dazzling snow-white 5-lobed pinwheel blossoms that glow luminous in the moonlight.
identifyingFeatures: Pure white 5-lobed corolla with lobes curving or twisted like a children's pinwheel toy
Glossy, deep-green elliptic-oblong opposite leaves with prominent arched veins
Dichotomously branching stems exuding a white milky latex when snapped
Fragrant blossoms, especially in the evening and during warm monsoon nights
138.habitat: Home gardens, sacred temple groves, public parks, road dividers, and tropical shrub borders.
138.distribution: Native to India, Bangladesh, Nepal, and Southeast Asia; widely cultivated across tropical regions.
uses: Sacred flowering shrub across India, flowers widely plucked for daily puja and temple worship
Traditional Ayurvedic remedies utilize milky latex for eye inflammation and root decoctions for toothache
Standard landscaping hedge and foundation planting providing dependable white blooms year-round
careTips: Thrives in full sun to partial afternoon shade; requires at least 4 hours of sun for rich blooming
Maintain consistently moist, organically rich, well-draining soil
Prune after the monsoon flowering flush to maintain a compact, bushy rounded shrub
138.toxicityNote: MILDLY TOXIC: All plant parts contain indole alkaloids (coronaridine, voacangine). The white latex can cause eye irritation; ingestion causes nausea and vomiting in pets.
138.funFact: In Hindi it is poetically called 'Chandni' (Moonlight) because its radiant white pinwheel blossoms appear to shine like scattered stars under a full moon.

139.description: A fast-growing, sun-loving ornamental shrub or small tree bearing dense terminal clusters of luminous golden-yellow trumpet-shaped blossoms with subtle orange-red throat markings and serrated pinnate foliage.
identifyingFeatures: Large clusters of brilliant golden-yellow bell-to-trumpet flowers with faint red interior throat guidelines
Opposite pinnately compound leaves with 5 to 13 sharply serrated (toothed) lanceolate leaflets
Long, slender dangling bean-like brown seed capsules (10–20 cm) containing winged seeds
Upright branching woody shrub habit reaching 4–6 meters if left unpruned
139.habitat: Roadside verges, highway dividers, urban park borders, dry rocky slopes, and home gardens.
139.distribution: Native to the Americas (Texas and Florida to Argentina); naturalized and widespread in urban areas across India.
uses: One of the most resilient and drought-hardy street landscaping plants, extensively planted on urban highway medians
Continuous nectar and pollen buffet for honeybees, bumblebees, sunbirds, and butterflies
Traditional Mexican herbal remedies use leaf teas for managing diabetes (tecomine alkaloid)
careTips: Requires full, blazing sun for heavy flowering; flowers poorly in shade
Extremely drought-tolerant once established; water only when the topsoil is completely dry
Prune spent flower clusters and dangling seed pods to stimulate rapid re-blooming
139.toxicityNote: NON-TOXIC to humans under normal landscape handling. Contains alkaloids that may cause mild stomach upset if foliage is eaten by livestock in huge quantities.
139.funFact: Tecoma stans is the official national flower of the Bahamas and the official floral emblem of the United States Virgin Islands.

140.description: A striking succulent shrub featuring a swollen, sculpted basal water-storage trunk (caudex) resembling a natural bonsai, topped with spirals of glossy leathery leaves and flamboyant trumpet flowers in shades of pink, red, and white.
identifyingFeatures: Massively swollen, grotesque or sculptured succulent basal stem (caudex) storing water
Vivid 5-lobed bell-shaped flowers in red, rose-pink, or white, often with contrasting margins or centers
Glossy, leathery spiraling oblanceolate leaves clustered at the branch tips
Stout fleshy branches exuding a clear or milky sap when broken
140.habitat: Arid scrublands, rocky desert hillsides, succulent container gardens, and balcony collections.
140.distribution: Native to the Sahel region of Africa (Mauritania to Somalia) and Arabian Peninsula; prized globally by succulent hobbyists.
uses: One of the world's most prized flowering succulent bonsai plants, sculpted into unique living art forms
High-heat tolerant container plant for sunny balconies, terraces, and desert landscapes
Historical use of concentrated sap as an arrow poison by traditional hunters in Africa
careTips: Requires full intense sunlight (at least 6 hours daily); insufficient light prevents blooming and weakens the caudex
Plant in an ultra-porous cactus potting mix (gravel, perlite, coarse sand, and pumice)
Water thoroughly in summer only when soil is bone dry; reduce watering almost completely during winter dormancy
140.toxicityNote: HIGHLY TOXIC: The sap contains potent cardiac glycosides (including ouabain). Ingestion causes severe cardiac arrhythmias, vomiting, diarrhea, and can be fatal to pets.
140.funFact: In indigenous African tribal hunting, the toxic sap was boiled down to create a lethal arrow poison used to bring down large game like antelopes and elephants.

141.description: A sprawling woody evergreen shrub celebrated across South Asia for slender tubular greenish-white flowers that open after sunset to release an overwhelming, intoxicatingly sweet nocturnal fragrance that can drift hundreds of meters.
identifyingFeatures: Clusters of slender, tubular greenish-white to pale cream flowers that open exclusively at night
Intense, pervasive sweet perfume released after dusk that fills the surrounding night air
Smooth, lanceolate alternate glossy green leaves with entire margins
Small globular white berries containing toxic seeds
141.habitat: Residential gardens, courtyard corners, near bedroom windows, and park borders.
141.distribution: Native to the West Indies and Central America; deeply naturalized and ubiquitous across India and South Asia.
uses: Renowned fragrant garden shrub traditionally planted near bedroom verandas and courtyard sitting areas
Night pollinators feast: magnetically attracts hawkmoths, sphinx moths, and nocturnal insects
Popular ornamental shrub for tropical and subtropical border plantings
careTips: Plant in full sun to partial shade in well-draining garden soil
Provide regular watering during warm growing months; mulch to keep root zone cool
Prune back heavily after flowering flushes to prevent lanky growth and encourage fresh flowering stems
141.toxicityNote: TOXIC: All parts of the plant—especially the white berries—contain solanine and atropine-like alkaloids. Ingestion causes fever, rapid pulse, dizziness, hallucinations, and vomiting.
141.funFact: Despite its common Hindi name 'Raat ki Rani' and English name 'Night-blooming Jasmine', it is not a true jasmine (Oleaceae) but a member of the nightshade family (Solanaceae), closely related to tomatoes and potatoes.

142.description: A low-growing, sun-worshipping succulent annual ground cover with cylindrical fleshy leaves and brilliant rose-like blossoms in dazzling shades of magenta, red, orange, yellow, and white that open wide under bright morning sun.
identifyingFeatures: Showy cup-shaped or rose-like ruffled flowers in dazzling colors that open in morning sunlight and close by late afternoon
Fleshy, cylindrical (terete) needle-like succulent leaves arranged alternately along reddish stems
Low-creeping, mat-forming habit rarely exceeding 15 cm in height
Small cup-shaped capsule containing tiny, iridescent metallic black seeds
142.habitat: Sunny rock gardens, balcony planters, edge borders, hanging baskets, and sandy dry soil.
142.distribution: Native to Argentina, southern Brazil, and Uruguay; grown universally in warm climates around the globe.
uses: Exceptional heat-tolerant annual carpet bedding for blazing sunny borders and rockeries
Ideal for shallow balcony bowls, hanging baskets, and rooftop garden containers
Provides vital morning nectar for small solitary bees, honeybees, and skippers
careTips: Requires absolute full sun; flowers will not open properly on cloudy days or in shaded locations
Prefers lean, gritty, well-draining sandy soil; over-fertilizing causes lush foliage with few flowers
Water sparingly; extremely drought-tolerant and susceptible to stem rot if over-watered
142.toxicityNote: MILDLY TOXIC TO PETS: Contains soluble calcium oxalates. Ingestion in significant amounts can cause drooling, vomiting, and tremors in cats and dogs.
142.funFact: Known widely across India as 'Nau Bajiya' (9 o'clock) or 'Das Bajiya' (10 o'clock) because its flowers open with clockwork precision as soon as the morning sun strikes the petals.

143.description: A beloved bushy herbaceous perennial celebrated for its electrifying, kaleidoscopic velvet-textured leaves combining vivid shades of magenta, chartreuse, lime green, burgundy, copper, and cream.
identifyingFeatures: Square, succulent four-angled stems typical of the mint family (Lamiaceae)
Opposite ovate leaves with serrated margins, displaying kaleidoscopic multicolored color patterns
Velvety soft leaf texture with contrasting colored margins or center blotches
Upright terminal spikes of tiny two-lipped pale blue to purple flowers
143.habitat: Tropical forest borders, garden flower beds, balcony containers, and bright indoor spaces.
143.distribution: Native to Southeast Asia through Australia; cultivated worldwide as one of the most diverse foliage plants.
uses: Top bedding and container plant offering continuous explosive color without depending on blooms
Popular houseplant for bright windowsills, living walls, and plant arrangements
Effortless water propagation: stem cuttings root in water within a few days
careTips: Enjoys bright indirect sunlight or gentle morning sun; harsh hot sun can scorch leaves or bleach colors
Keep soil consistently moist but never soggy; wilts dramatically when thirsty but recovers quickly upon watering
Pinch off flower spikes as they appear to redirect plant energy toward dense, colorful leaf production
143.toxicityNote: MILDLY TOXIC TO PETS: Contains essential oils and diterpenes. Can cause mild vomiting, diarrhea, and lethargy if chewed by dogs or cats.
143.funFact: Coleus exhibits one of the most diverse arrays of leaf color variations in the entire plant kingdom, with hundreds of named varieties created through centuries of botanical breeding.

144.description: A fast-growing evergreen tropical shrub boasting large, heart-shaped serrated leaves splashed with an eye-catching blend of coppery green, bronze, fiery red, rose-pink, and creamy white margins.
identifyingFeatures: Broadly ovate, coarsely toothed leaves with an iridescent coppery-red, bronze, or crimson mottled coloration
Inconspicuous, drooping catkin-like spikes of tiny reddish flowers hidden among foliage
Erect, bushy branching woody shrub habit reaching 2 to 3 meters in height
Foliage color intensifies in full sun and warmer temperatures
144.habitat: Tropical shrub borders, residential foundation plantings, park hedges, and coastal landscapes.
144.distribution: Native to Fiji and adjacent South Pacific islands; widely grown as a hedging shrub across the tropics.
uses: Top-tier hedging and border shrub providing continuous vibrant coppery-crimson foliage
Accent specimen for tropical and subtropical landscaping
Traditional Polynesian folk medicine used leaf decoctions for soothing skin dermatoses
careTips: Plant in full sun to partial shade; full sun produces the richest, most vibrant foliage colors
Water regularly to keep soil moist; benefits from organic mulching around the root zone
Prune back in early spring to encourage dense branching and lush new brightly colored shoots
144.toxicityNote: MILDLY TOXIC: Sap can cause mild skin irritation and redness. Ingestion may cause mild gastrointestinal upset in household pets.
144.funFact: Named in honor of Admiral Charles Wilkes (1798–1877), the American naval officer and explorer who commanded the historic United States Exploring Expedition to the South Pacific.

145.description: A spiny, drought-hardy semi-succulent shrub bearing sharp woody thorns, obovate bright green leaves, and long-lasting pairs of vivid petal-like floral bracts (cyathia) in brilliant scarlet, pink, or yellow.
identifyingFeatures: Dense, sharp straight woody spines (up to 3 cm long) covering stout, grooved gray-brown succulent stems
Pairs of bright petal-like modified bracts (cyathia) in crimson red, salmon, or yellow surrounding tiny true flowers
Tear-drop shaped obovate green leaves clustered predominantly near stem tips
Copious poisonous white milky latex exuded whenever any stem, leaf, or spine is damaged
145.habitat: Rocky granite slopes, arid scrublands, balcony containers, rockeries, and security hedges.
145.distribution: Native to Madagascar; cultured globally as a virtually indestructible flowering succulent.
uses: Outstanding flowering succulent for full-sun containers, desert landscapes, and sunny balconies
Virtually year-round continuous blooming in frost-free tropical environments
Planted as an impenetrable thorny barrier hedge along property boundaries
careTips: Requires full direct sunlight (at least 4–6 hours daily) for profuse, vibrant flowering
Plant in fast-draining cactus and succulent mix; water thoroughly only when soil is completely dry
Wear protective gloves when pruning to avoid contact with the caustic, skin-blistering white milky sap
145.toxicityNote: HIGHLY TOXIC: The milky sap contains caustic phorbol esters. Contact causes intense skin burning, blistering, and temporary blindness if rubbed into eyes. Ingestion causes severe burning of mouth and stomach.
145.funFact: Legend claims that the thorny branches of this Madagascan succulent were used to weave the crown of thorns placed on Jesus Christ during the Crucifixion, giving rise to its enduring common name.

146.description: A sprawling evergreen scrambling shrub celebrated for profuse, rounded trusses of delicate phlox-like sky-blue or baby-blue flowers that bloom almost continuously through warm weather.
identifyingFeatures: Spherical clusters of 5-petaled sky-blue flowers (rarely white) with a slender floral tube
Floral calyces covered in sticky, gland-tipped hairs that catch on clothing and animal fur
Alternate, oblong-spathulate bright green leaves with small ear-like stipules (auricles) at petiole bases
Sprawling, arching woody stems capable of scrambling up fences or spilling over retaining walls
146.habitat: Coastal scrub, dry hillsides, garden borders, retaining walls, and sunny balconies.
146.distribution: Native to South Africa; widely cultivated and naturalized across India and warm regions globally.
uses: Premier blue-flowering landscape shrub for sunny banks, retaining walls, and cascading hedges
One of the few reliable sources of true sky-blue floral coloration in tropical horticulture
Larval host plant for the common zebra blue butterfly (Leptotes plinius)
careTips: Thrives in full blazing sun; flowering decreases noticeably in shady positions
Extremely heat and drought-tolerant once established in well-draining garden soil
Prune hard in late winter or early spring to remove woody tangles and stimulate energetic new blooming shoots
146.toxicityNote: MILDLY TOXIC: Sap contains plumbagin, which can cause skin irritation, blistering, and dermatitis upon prolonged contact. Ingestion causes nausea.
146.funFact: The sticky glandular hairs on the calyces trap small insects, a trait historically thought to protect developing seeds or represent proto-carnivorous behavior.

147.description: A tough, drought-resilient large evergreen shrub native to India, renowned for thick waxy leaves covered in white woolly pubescence and extraordinary crown-like lilac-purple or white flowers sacred in Hindu rituals.
identifyingFeatures: Unique star-shaped flowers with a prominent raised central five-pointed crown (corona) in lilac, lavender, or white
Large, thick, leathery obovate-oblong leaves with a glaucous blue-green tint and fine white downy coating
Stems and leaves exude a copious, highly irritating white milky latex when bruised
Boat-shaped curved, inflated follicle pods that split open to release seeds attached to silky white tufts
147.habitat: Arid wasteland, sandy coastal dunes, roadside ditches, dry scrublands, and sacred temple grounds.
147.distribution: Native to India, Sri Lanka, Nepal, China, and Southeast Asia; naturalized in tropical arid regions worldwide.
uses: Sacred ritual flower across India, flowers offered to Lord Shiva and Lord Hanuman
Crucial larval food plant for the majestic plain tiger butterfly (Danaus chrysippus)
Stem fibers yield exceptionally durable, water-resistant cordage traditionally used for fishing nets and bowstrings
Extensive use in traditional Ayurveda (Arka) for skin ailments, rheumatism, and counter-irritants (under expert supervision)
careTips: Thrives in full scorching sun and poor sandy or gravelly soils where other plants perish
Virtually immune to drought once rooted; never requires supplementary irrigation in garden settings
Wear gloves and protective goggles when trimming to safeguard against caustic milky sap
147.toxicityNote: HIGHLY TOXIC: Milky latex contains potent cardenolides (calotropin, calotoxin). Ingestion can cause fatal heart attacks, vomiting, and convulsions. Contact with eyes causes severe corneal damage and temporary blindness.
147.funFact: The silky white floss attached to Calotropis seeds was traditionally gathered in rural India to stuff soft pillows and mattresses because it is naturally water-repellent and resistant to insects.

148.description: A graceful, vigorous sprawling evergreen shrub or small tree featuring arching branches hung with cascading racemes of soft lavender-blue flowers, followed by drooping clusters of lustrous golden-orange berries.
identifyingFeatures: Cascading terminal panicles of dainty, 5-lobed sky-blue or lilac flowers with wavy white petal borders
Heavy hanging clusters of bright golden-yellow to orange globular berries (golden dewdrops) persisting on branches
Opposite, bright green elliptic to ovate leaves, frequently accompanied by sharp axillary spines on older stems
Arching, drooping branches creating a fountain-like weeping shrub habit
148.habitat: Residential gardens, park hedges, roadside dividers, and coastal hillsides.
148.distribution: Native to the tropical Americas (Florida and West Indies to Brazil); planted universally across India.
uses: One of the most popular formal hedge and privacy screening shrubs in Indian urban gardens
High nectar production attracts abundant swallowtails, skippers, and honeybees
Weeping fountain specimen for large lawn containers and patio backgrounds
careTips: Plant in full sun to maximize blooming cascades and dense golden berry clusters
Tolerates diverse soil types as long as drainage is adequate; fairly drought-hardy once rooted
Responds exceptionally well to heavy shearing and topiary shaping
148.toxicityNote: TOXIC: The attractive golden berries and foliage contain saponins and cardiac glycosides. Ingestion of berries can cause fever, nausea, vomiting, convulsions, and has caused fatalities in small pets and children.
148.funFact: Called 'Golden dewdrop' because the heavy clusters of bright orange-yellow berries look like shimmering golden drops of morning dew dangling along weeping branches.

149.description: A magnificent large tropical deciduous tree renowned for cauliflory, producing huge, sweetly scented bizarre pink-orange blossoms that emerge directly from tangled woody racemes on the trunk, followed by large heavy spherical wooden cannonballs.
identifyingFeatures: Cauliflorous habit: large exotic flowers and heavy cannonball fruits borne on woody tangled racemes emerging directly from the main trunk
Striking, deeply fragrant flowers (up to 10 cm) with 6 thick salmon-pink concave petals and a curving hood-like white-and-pink staminal ring resembling a cobra protecting a Shiva lingam
Enormous spherical, woody brown fruits (15–24 cm diameter) resembling iron cannonballs
Dense crown of obovate leaves clustered at branch ends, shed completely several times a year
149.habitat: Sacred Hindu temple grounds, botanical gardens, royal palace parks, and tropical rainforests.
149.distribution: Native to the Guianas and tropical South America; revered and extensively planted around Shiva temples across India and Sri Lanka.
uses: Sacred tree planted beside Shiva temples across South India; flowers revered as divine symbols of the Shivalinga hooded by the serpent Shesha
Spectacular botanical curiosity planted in major botanical gardens and university campuses worldwide
Traditional Amazonian remedies utilize bark decoctions for malaria and skin infections
careTips: Requires expansive outdoor space away from walkways and parked cars due to heavy falling cannonball fruits
Thrives in rich, humid, deep alluvial soils in warm tropical climates
Needs full sunlight to support large canopy growth and prolific cauliflorous blooming
149.toxicityNote: NON-TOXIC flowers. However, falling mature cannonball fruits can weigh up to 3 kg and pose severe physical impact hazard to people walking underneath. The fruit pulp has an unpleasant pungent smell when broken.
149.funFact: In India, the tree is known as 'Nagalingam' because the central curved staminal hood mirrors a many-headed cobra (Naga) shielding the sacred Shiva Lingam resting on the floral disc.
